docs.title: langchain-cockroachdb
docs.text: LangChain integration for CockroachDB with native vector support

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This package provides LangChain abstractions backed by CockroachDB, leveraging CockroachDB's native VECTOR type and C-SPANN (CockroachDB SPANN) indexes for vector search at scale in a distributed, horizontally scalable database.

docs.title: 🎯 Vector Store
docs.text:
• Native Vector Support: Uses CockroachDB's native VECTOR type (not pgvector)
  • C-SPANN Indexes: CockroachDB's vector index algorithm optimized for distributed systems
  • Advanced Filtering: Rich metadata filtering with $and/$or/$gt/$in operators
  • Hybrid Search: Combine full-text search (TSVECTOR) with vector similarity
  • Query-Time Tuning: Adjust beam size for accuracy/speed tradeoff

docs.title: 🏗️ Reliability Features
docs.text:
• Automatic Retry Logic: Retries transient CockroachDB errors (40001, 40003, 08xxx, 57P01, 58C00, 58C01) on every operation
  • Isolation Level Support: Works with both SERIALIZABLE (default, recommended) and READ COMMITTED
  • Multi-Tenancy: Namespace-based isolation with C-SPANN prefix columns
  • Connection Pooling: Configurable connection pools with health checks
  • Horizontal Scalability: Designed for distributed deployments

docs.title: 💬 Chat History
docs.text:
• Persistent Storage: Store conversation history in CockroachDB
  • Session Management: Organize by session/thread ID
  • LangChain Integration: Drop-in replacement for other chat history implementations

docs.title: 🧠 LangGraph Checkpointer
docs.text:
• Short-Term Memory: Persist agent state across conversation turns
  • Human-in-the-Loop: Interrupt and resume workflows with durable state
  • Fault Tolerance: Recover from process restarts without losing progress
  • Sync & Async: Both CockroachDBSaver and AsyncCockroachDBSaver

docs.title: LangGraph Long-Term Memory
docs.text:
• Long-Term Memory: Memory that every thread can read, for LangGraph agents and Deep Agents
  • Semantic Search: C-SPANN vector index with the namespace as a prefix column
  • Expiry: CockroachDB row-level TTL deletes expired memories, with no sweeper thread
  • Sync & Async: Both CockroachDBStore and AsyncCockroachDBStore

docs.title: 🔄 Async & Sync APIs
docs.text:
• Async-First: High-performance async operations for I/O concurrency
  • Sync Wrapper: Simple synchronous API for scripts and batch jobs
  • Connection Pooling: Efficient connection reuse across async operations

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
import asyncio
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore, CockroachDBEngine
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings

async def main():
    # Initialize engine
    engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(
        "cockroachdb://user:pass@host:26257/db?sslmode=verify-full"
    )

    # Create table
    await engine.ainit_vectorstore_table(
        table_name="documents",
        vector_dimension=1536,
    )

    # Initialize vector store
    vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
        engine=engine,
        embeddings=OpenAIEmbeddings(),
        collection_name="documents",
    )

    # Add documents
    await vectorstore.aadd_texts([
        "CockroachDB is a distributed SQL database",
        "LangChain makes it easy to build LLM applications",
    ])

    # Search
    results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(
        "Tell me about databases",
        k=2
    )

    print(results)
    await engine.aclose()

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Why CockroachDB?
docs.text:
• Distributed by Design: Scale horizontally across regions
  • Native Vector Support: First-class VECTOR type and C-SPANN indexes
  • Strong Consistency: SERIALIZABLE by default, READ COMMITTED also supported
  • Cloud Native: Deploy anywhere (AWS, GCP, Azure, on-prem)
  • PostgreSQL Compatible: Familiar SQL with distributed superpowers

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Memory reconciliation on CockroachDBStore and AsyncCockroachDBStore, to keep long-term memory true. reconcile(namespace, key, value, policy=...) writes a memory and, in one serializable transaction, finds the memories it may conflict with, runs the application's policy on them, and supersedes, deletes, confirms or keeps each one. The candidates are the live memory under the same key, the memories whose value holds the same slot value, and on a store with an index those whose vectors score at or above threshold. That is 0.8 by default on a cosine store, and must be given on an l2 or inner_product store. The candidates are read in the transaction that writes, so two agents that reconcile contradictory memories for one user cannot both win. find_conflicts and resolve do the same in two steps, so an LLM or a person can decide while no transaction is open. resolve checks that the memories the decision depends on still have the version and updated_at that find_conflicts read. If one changed, it raises ConflictsChanged and writes nothing. The built-in policies are supersede_same_slot(), skip_duplicates(), supersede_similar(), keep_all() and first_of(), and reconcile has no default policy. skip_duplicates() skips a new memory that repeats one already stored, and confirms that memory. With a slot, only a memory in the same slot counts as a repeat, so a repeat outside the slot never keeps an older memory in the slot live. For a key that holds a live memory, it skips only a save of the same value, and never an update to another value, which first_of passes to the next policy. The store setting reconcile_scan_limit (default 2000) is the most vectors a namespace may hold for its similar candidates to be ranked exactly. A larger namespace takes them from the C-SPANN index.
  • Version history, turned on with history=True or history={"ttl_days": ...} on the store and on from_conn_string. setup() then creates <table>_history. Every write that overwrites, supersedes or deletes a memory keeps the version it ends, in the same transaction, with when its fact was true, why it ended, what replaced it and its provenance. That includes plain put and delete, so LangMem-style tools, which write through them, get history too. With history on, delete is a soft delete. purge(namespace, key) removes a memory with its vectors and its history, delete_namespace removes the history under the prefix too, even on a store created without history when the history table exists, and history(namespace, key) lists a memory's old versions. Without a key, history(namespace) lists the old versions of every memory in the namespace, newest first, each with its key and superseded_by, so the old versions of memories saved under generated keys can be found too. limit and offset page through both forms.
  • Provenance and valid time. reconcile, find_conflicts and put_if take provenance, any JSON object, kept in its own column, and valid_at, when the fact became true. Without valid_at the valid time comes from the database's clock. Of the built-in policies, only supersede_same_slot() and supersede_similar() compare valid times: a fact that arrives late is recorded as superseded instead of replacing a newer one, and a late fact under its own live key is skipped, not recorded. record(namespace, key) returns a live memory with its version, provenance, valid time and confirmations.
  • confirm(namespace, key, ttl=...) marks a memory as confirmed. It renews the expiry, from the memory's own TTL or from minutes, None or a function of the memory, and counts the confirmation. Confirmations belong to the fact: a write that changes the value starts them again from none, an exact re-save keeps them, and history keeps each version's count. record and find_conflicts never push back an expiry, and with refresh_on_read=False expiry follows confirmations rather than reads.
  • Conditional writes. put_if(namespace, key, value, expected=record) and delete_if(namespace, key, expected=record) apply only if the memory is still the one record returned, and expected=None creates a memory only if none is live under the key. A conflict is returned, not raised: the ConditionalWrite result has applied=False and current, the live memory, to merge with.
  • The async store has each of these methods as a coroutine with an a prefix. The new types and policies are exported from langchain_cockroachdb.store: Proposal, Candidate, Decision, Action, Conflicts, ConflictsChanged, ReconcileResult, MemoryRecord, MemoryVersion, ConditionalWrite, HistoryConfig, Policy and validate_decision. RECONCILE_SERDE_TYPES, exported there too, lists the classes these values hold, in the form that a checkpoint serializer's allowed_msgpack_modules takes from langgraph-checkpoint 4.0.1. With it, a Conflicts or a Decision can wait in graph state while a person decides.
  • What this does not do: the store makes no LLM calls, though a judge in the two-step flow may. It does not record TTL expiry in history either, since CockroachDB's TTL job deletes rows directly. A changefeed on the items table captures those deletes.
  • examples/memory_reconciliation.py, and a "Keeping memories true" section in the long-term memory guide, with an example page and API entries in the documentation.
  • A guide to virtual-cluster connections for the engine, chat history, the checkpointers and the store: a Cockroach Continuum virtual cluster's own connection string, or a self-hosted virtualized cluster selected with the percent-encoded options=-ccluster%3D<name>. Unit tests cover connection-string handling, and an opt-in suite checks that two virtual clusters keep their data apart.
  • Recovery tests for LangGraph graphs on pooled checkpointers: an application process that is killed and restarted in a fresh process, and a pooled connection lost while a graph runs. Graphs resume from their last saved checkpoint, a node that finished and saved its writes does not run again, and no checkpoint write is lost or duplicated.
  • A checkpointer guide section on LangGraph's durability modes. It explains that LangGraph's default, "async", can lose the last checkpoint and the tool call recorded in it when the process dies, why an idempotency key built from the tool-call ID does not catch the repeat that follows, and when to pass durability="sync".

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Upgrading from 0.5: run setup() once. It applies migration 2, which adds version, provenance, confirmed_at, confirmations, write_id, valid_at and confirm_id to the items table in one statement. On a large table, run it once from a single process before the rollout: the backfill takes longer the more items the table holds. When several processes run setup() at once, the statement from all but one returns at once, before the columns exist, so each of those waits until the columns are public and SHOW JOBS shows no schema change job on the table, for up to SCHEMA_CHANGE_SETTLE_SECONDS (10 minutes, exported), before it records migration 2. A store that finds migration 2 recorded then never writes columns that are not there yet. Two cases leave the columns alone to decide: SHOW JOBS shows a role without admin only its own jobs, and it can cut a long qualified table name from a job's description. If no job applies the migration, as after a peer's migration failed, the waiting setup() applies it itself and logs that at INFO. The wait logs an INFO line when it starts, a WARNING once it has waited SCHEMA_CHANGE_QUIET_SECONDS (30) and one a minute after that, and an INFO line when it ends. If it runs out, setup() raises TimeoutError saying what remained. The wait is not a retry, so max_attempts=1 does not shorten it. Until then the store works as 0.5 did, and the new methods raise ValueError asking for setup(). With history off and the new methods unused, the store behaves as in 0.5 apart from the new columns. During a rolling upgrade, 0.5 writers do not bump the version but do set updated_at, and resolve, put_if and delete_if check both. 0.5 writers never archive, and one that re-creates a deleted key starts it again at version 1, which history then cannot keep, since it already holds a version 1 of that key. So turn history on only once every writer runs 0.6.0. On the checkpointers, if you turned on row-level TTL, run enable_ttl() once more with the same interval and cron (see Fixed). That adds the grace for blob rows, stores months and years as days, and brings forward the blob rows of threads idle since the upgrade, pausing TTL while it does. It blocks for about 15 seconds plus the pass, so if startup probes are tight, run it once from a single process or a one-off job before the rollout. Until then, puts refresh blob rows, but a thread that has written since the upgrade can lose blob rows up to a tenth of the interval before its last checkpoint expires, a thread idle since the upgrade up to the whole interval before, and a setting in months or years is refreshed only approximately.
  • Least-privilege roles. An application role that did not run setup() needs SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the items and vectors tables, and on the history table when history is on. With history off, it still needs SELECT and DELETE on a history table left from when history was on, since delete_namespace deletes the namespace's rows there, and fails as a whole without them. The store now reads the migrations table before its first write, to learn whether migration 2 is in place. A role without SELECT on it, or a store whose tables were created without setup() and have no migrations table, reads the items table's columns instead. On a multi-node cluster such a role can fail one write in the seconds after setup() applies migration 2, so run setup() before rolling out 0.6.0, or grant SELECT on the migrations table. Without that grant, the first store call inside a transaction the caller opened gets the permission error, once per store. Only the grant avoids it.
  • A memory store semantic search takes at least 41 vectors from the C-SPANN index for its window, where it took twice the page. Finding 41 costs the index about the same as finding fewer: on a 20,000-row table it read about 10% more rows than a window of 9, in the same time. A larger window lets more filtered searches skip the exact second query.
  • The README and the docs site use the new Cockroach Labs logo, and the docs site has a favicon that follows the system theme.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A vector store search with a metadata filter now uses the C-SPANN index. CockroachDB uses a vector index only when every filter matches its prefix columns, so a filter made every filtered similarity_search and its variants, every filtered MMR search and the vector leg of every filtered hybrid search scan the table. With a usable index, the store now takes the nearest rows from the index (twice k plus one, and at least 41), applies the filter to them, and runs the exact search as before when fewer than k rows pass: always when none does, and when some do unless the window held every row of the table or namespace. The exact search returns only the store's namespace, but its plan can scan the whole table. A result that comes from the window is approximate, as every index search is, and the beam size sets how close it comes; filtered searches used to scan and were exact. In MMR search fetch_k takes the place of k, and in hybrid search so does its pool, fetch_k or max(4 * k, 20). A usable index is on the embedding column, has the operator class of the store's distance strategy, and has no prefix column for a store without a namespace, or the namespace column as its only prefix column for a namespaced store. A namespaced store also needs the primary key or an index to lead with the namespace column, as ainit_vectorstore_table creates, or it keeps the exact search. The store reads the table's indexes with SHOW CREATE TABLE on its first filtered search. The engine keeps the answer for every store on it with the same table, embedding column, distance strategy and namespace column, so a store built per request does not read again. It reads again once VECTOR_INDEX_REFRESH_SECONDS (60, exported) have passed, and right after an index is applied or dropped through any store on the engine. If that read fails with a database error that the retry policy does not retry, such as a missing privilege, the store logs it once at INFO and runs the exact search. Without a filter or a usable index, a search runs the same single statement as before. The vector indexes guide has a new section on filtered search. It now gives the default beam size as 32, says that prefix columns come only from prefix_columns and that a key in filter is never one, and warns that building an index on a table that holds data blocks writes to it until the backfill ends.
  • setup() run by several processes at once now converges, as when pods restart into 0.6.0 together. On CockroachDB v25.4 a TTL change fails while another schema change runs on the same table. While one process's migration 2 backfills the items table, which takes longer the more items it holds, the others go on to change its TTL settings. That error was retried under the store's retry policy, for about a second by default, so their setup() could fail. setup() now reads each table's TTL settings first and changes them only when they differ, so the processes after the first change nothing. And the error now has a retry budget sized for schema changes: each TTL change retries it for up to ten minutes of wall time by default, as long as a setup() waits for another process's migration, so it also waits out a long backfill or vector index build. A setup() can wait one such budget per table whose TTL it changes. It logs a WARNING on the first retry and at most one a minute after that. The same budget applies to the store's disable_ttl() and adisable_ttl(), and to enable_ttl() and disable_ttl() on the checkpointers and their async forms. Its defaults are exported as SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_SECONDS (600) and SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_MAX_BACKOFF (3 seconds), and schema_change_policy() takes seconds and max_backoff and keeps a RetryPolicy subclass's is_retryable and delay overrides for every other error. Other errors keep the policy's own attempts and backoff, and max_attempts=1 still turns every retry off.
  • Loading the state of a graph that uses LangGraph's DeltaChannel read the checkpoint history one checkpoint at a time. Deep Agents stores its messages and files in delta channels, which keep only each step's change and a full snapshot every 50 updates, so LangGraph asks the checkpointer for the history back to the last snapshot on every get_state and every resumed run. The checkpointers inherited LangGraph's default for that request, which calls get_tuple once per ancestor, three queries each. Loading a Deep Agent's state after four turns took 63 queries, and the count grew with every turn until the next snapshot. CockroachDBSaver and AsyncCockroachDBSaver now override get_delta_channel_history and aget_delta_channel_history. They follow the parent chain with a recursive query and load each page of ancestors in one batch, in pages that start at 16 ancestors and grow up to 256 (DELTA_HISTORY_FIRST_PAGE, DELTA_HISTORY_PAGE_SIZE). The result is the same as LangGraph's default, which the new tests check on every checkpoint of real graphs, including a forked thread.
  • A checkpoint's pending writes came back ordered by task_id, a hash, instead of LangGraph's writes_sort_key order (task_path, task_id, idx). LangGraph replays stored writes in the order the checkpointer returns them, so when parallel tasks in one step wrote the same channel, state rebuilt after a reload could differ from the state the run produced. With a DeltaChannel, such as Deep Agents' messages and files, a reloaded list could come back in a different order. get_tuple, list and their async versions now return pending writes in writes_sort_key order.
  • Row-level TTL on the checkpointers could delete values that an active thread still used. enable_ttl() expires each row by its own created_at. A blob row holds one channel version and is written once, so a channel that had not changed since an early step, such as a profile set on the first turn, kept its first blob row, which every newer checkpoint used. Once that row was older than the interval, the TTL job deleted it, and the value dropped out of the thread's state without an error. On an idle thread, blob rows could also expire before the checkpoint that used them. With TTL on, put and aput now bring created_at forward on the blob rows the new checkpoint uses but does not write, once they are older than a tenth of the interval (TTL_REFRESH_FRACTION, 10), in the same transaction as the checkpoint. enable_ttl() gives blob rows that tenth as a grace, (created_at + interval + interval / 10), keeps checkpoints and writes at (created_at + interval), stores months and years as days, 30 to a month and 365 to a year, since calendar months differ in length and no grace could cover them, and refuses an interval longer than 106,751 days, the longest duration CockroachDB keeps. When it turns TTL on or changes it, it first writes the new settings with TTL paused (ttl_pause), so nothing is deleted, and waits TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS (10) plus TTL_PAUSE_MARGIN_SECONDS (5), or plus the retry policy's attempt_timeout when that is longer, so that every saver reads the new setting and the puts already under way finish; savers refresh while TTL is paused. Then it makes one pass, so threads idle at that moment are covered too: each blob row that checkpoints inside the interval use, and that is older than the newest of them by more than the window, is brought forward to now. Only rows left unchanged that long are rewritten, not the table. The pass reads every checkpoint once, TTL_REFRESH_BATCH_SIZE (500) at a time, changes at most TTL_REFRESH_UPDATE_SIZE (100) rows per UPDATE, each its own short statement under the retry policy's ddl_attempt_timeout, and logs at INFO when it starts and ends. Then it reads the setting again and resumes TTL, checkpoint_blobs last, unless another run has written a different setting meanwhile: it leaves the resume to that run and logs at INFO. CockroachDB may skip its next scheduled TTL job once after the resume, with "found a recent schema change", which delays deletion by one cron period. So whenever the setting changes, enable_ttl() blocks for about 15 seconds on a table of any size, plus the pass, the first call after upgrading included, and it returns at once when the same setting is in place and running; any other change makes the whole run, a longer interval too. A run that stops before it resumes TTL leaves it paused, which deletes nothing. One that stops during the resume leaves only checkpoint_blobs paused, so checkpoints and writes expire again while blob rows stay, which only leaves behind blob rows that no checkpoint uses. The next enable_ttl() finishes either, and a saver that finds TTL paused logs a WARNING once per process each time, saying to run enable_ttl() again if no run is under way. disable_ttl() and then enable_ttl() force a pass. If startup probes are tight, run enable_ttl() once from a single process or a one-off job before a rollout. Use one interval in every process, and change it from one process. So once enable_ttl() has run, a blob row expires no earlier than the newest checkpoint that uses it, and a thread expires once it has been idle for the interval. The savers read the TTL setting of checkpoint_blobs from the catalog on the first put that needs it, and again after TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS (10) or right after their own enable_ttl() or disable_ttl(). Each attempt of a put decides again whether to refresh, so a retry made after the saver learns that TTL is on refreshes too. A TTL setting that enable_ttl() did not write turns the refresh off and is logged at INFO once per process. If that read fails with a database error that the retry policy does not retry, such as a missing privilege, puts go on without the refresh, and the saver logs a WARNING once. While TTL is on, a put that uses blob rows it does not write sends one more UPDATE in its transaction, and a blob row is rewritten at most once per tenth of the interval. Graphs that use DeltaChannel rebuild state from older checkpoints, which TTL still expires by age, so get_delta_channel_history now logs a WARNING, once per missing checkpoint and saver, when that history stops at a missing checkpoint before a snapshot. The checkpointer guide's TTL section says what TTL expires and covers both cases.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A checkpointer or store could fail with prepared statement "_pg3_N" does not exist (SQLSTATE 26000) after a batch failed before its statements ran, even when the error that failed the batch was retryable. psycopg prepares a statement on its sixth run on a connection (prepare_threshold=5, the default), and in pipeline mode it records the statement as prepared before the server confirms it. When an earlier statement in the batch failed, such as BEGIN refused by CockroachDB's license limit, the server never prepared it, but psycopg kept using it. A checkpoint write then failed on its retry. A store read failed on that connection every time until the connection closed, so a pool could hand out the broken connection until it was replaced, by default within an hour. Statements sent in a pipeline are no longer prepared. Statements outside a pipeline, such as the checkpointers' reads on a pool or on a connection without pipeline=True, still are, and every connection keeps its own prepare_threshold.
  • examples/long_term_memory.py and the store guide no longer print pydantic serializer warnings. Their tools now annotate the runtime as ToolRuntime[Context, dict]. A plain ToolRuntime expects no context, and ToolRuntime[Context] fails on Python 3.10, which cannot fill in the default of the second type argument.
  • The checkpointer guide said PostgresSaver's prepare_threshold=0 turns prepared statements off. It prepares every query from its first run.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• CockroachDBStore and AsyncCockroachDBStore, LangGraph long-term memory stores on CockroachDB. They implement LangGraph's BaseStore with the API of langgraph-checkpoint-postgres's PostgresStore (from_conn_string with pipeline and pool_config, setup(), index and ttl), so they work with create_agent(store=...), StateGraph.compile(store=...) and Deep Agents' StoreBackend. from_conn_string also takes retry_policy, connect_timeout, prepare_threshold and connect_kwargs, as the checkpointers do. The two stores, CockroachDBIndexConfig, CockroachDBTTLConfig and PoolConfig are exported from langchain_cockroachdb.store, and all of them but PoolConfig from langchain_cockroachdb too.
  • Semantic search on CockroachDB's VECTOR type, with a C-SPANN index that has the namespace as a prefix column. index takes LangGraph's dims, embed and fields, plus distance_type (cosine, l2 or inner_product), cspann partition sizes, flat to skip the index, and beam_size, which is set for each search. A search under a namespace first lists the namespaces at or under it, then ranks with the index within them, and runs a second, exact query when a filter or expired items leave its page short, unless a count shows that the index returned every vector of those namespaces. A search of the whole store, every search of a flat store, and a search over more than 1000 namespaces (MAX_SEARCH_NAMESPACES) rank every match exactly instead. So a filter or expired items never leave a page short while more matches exist.
  • Expiry through CockroachDB row-level TTL. With a ttl configuration, setup() turns on the TTL job for the items and vectors tables, on a schedule from sweep_interval_minutes or ttl_job_cron (@hourly by default), so no sweeper thread is needed. Vectors carry their item's expiry. Expired items are left out of reads, searches and listings by default, even by a store built without ttl; ttl={"omit_expired": False} turns that off. With refresh_on_read, a read pushes back the expiry of the items it returns, in the same statement. sweep_ttl(), start_ttl_sweeper() and stop_ttl_sweeper() work as in PostgresStore. A store built without ttl applies no default expiry, never refreshes one, and its setup() leaves an existing TTL setting alone. On CockroachDB v25.4, disable_ttl(), adisable_ttl() and the TTL step of setup() retry while another process changes the same table.
  • delete_namespace(namespace_prefix) and adelete_namespace, which delete every item and vector in a namespace and its descendants in one transaction and return the number of items deleted.
  • The sync methods of AsyncCockroachDBStore (batch, get, put, search, delete and list_namespaces) raise RuntimeError instead of hanging when the store's event loop is closed or not running, or when called from a forked child, as those of AsyncCockroachDBSaver do. From the loop's own thread they raise asyncio.InvalidStateError.
  • Differences from PostgresStore: the puts and deletes of one batch commit in one transaction; every call retries transient errors under the store's RetryPolicy; a CockroachDBStore on a pool runs batches concurrently; putting an item again or deleting it removes its old vectors; a filter that compares with a number matches numeric values only (PostgresStore compares text), nested dictionaries match nested keys, and $ne matches items without the key; results with the same score or updated_at are ordered by namespace and key, so paging is stable; table_name and schema configure the tables (defaults store, store_vectors and store_migrations in public); a query on a store without index logs a WARNING and runs a plain search; after setup(), a changed dims or distance_type raises, and other partition sizes, or flat with an index present, log a WARNING; disable_ttl() and adisable_ttl() remove the table TTL setting, and drop_vector_index() and adrop_vector_index() drop the vector index so that setup() can build it again, for example with another distance; and there is no deserializer= argument, because psycopg decodes JSONB before the store sees it.
  • examples/long_term_memory.py, a LangGraph agent that saves a memory in one thread and recalls it in another, and a guide, an example page and an API page for the store in the documentation.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• enable_ttl and disable_ttl (and aenable_ttl and adisable_ttl) on the checkpointers no longer fail when several processes run them at once on CockroachDB v25.4. That version refuses to change a table's TTL settings while another schema change on it runs, with SQLSTATE 0A000, which was not retried. These TTL changes now retry that error under the saver's retry policy, even if its retry_on would refuse it; max_attempts=1 turns this off. The code and phrase are exported as SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_SQLSTATE and SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_MESSAGES, with is_schema_change_busy() and schema_change_policy().
  • A checkpointer or store on one connection in pipeline mode (pipe=, or from_conn_string(..., pipeline=True)) could hang when a large write met a slow link, such as TLS to a distant cluster. psycopg's pipeline sync can leave the last bytes of a write unsent, so the server waited for them while the client waited for the server. The library now sends them before it waits. CockroachDBSaver and AsyncCockroachDBSaver had this since 0.2.0; CockroachDBStore and AsyncCockroachDBStore have the fix from the start. Pools, and single connections without a pipeline, were not affected.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: • Checkpointers on a psycopg_pool pool now run operations concurrently, each on its own pooled connection, so one saver can serve many agents, threads or tasks. Before, every operation in the process waited on one lock, which on a multi-region cluster capped a saver at a few operations per second. A saver on a single connection (including pipeline=True) still runs one operation at a time. Concurrency is bounded by the pool's max_size; when every connection is busy, operations wait for the pool (30 s by default) and a PoolTimeout is not retried. On a 9-node, 3-region CockroachDB cluster (Docker, with simulated cross-region latency and a stubbed model) with 16 LangGraph agents sharing one pooled saver, throughput went from 0.27 turns per second (median turn 55 s) in 0.4.0 to about 7.5 turns per second (median turn about 1.2 s) in 0.4.1.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• put with channel blobs, put_writes with several writes, and delete_thread now send BEGIN, their statements and COMMIT as one batch, so each write is saved completely or not at all, even when the caller is cancelled or fails partway. Before, an interrupted write could leave blob rows without their checkpoint, part of a task's pending writes (which LangGraph treats as a finished task), or a half-deleted thread. A write still takes one round trip, and CockroachDB can still retry it on the server. Single-statement writes are unchanged. Connections not in autocommit mode use psycopg's conn.transaction() (the docs already require autocommit=True).
  • On a single connection that the caller also uses, a write made inside a transaction the caller opened joins it as a savepoint, so the caller's commit or rollback decides. The saver never rolls back a transaction it did not open, and an error inside the caller's transaction is raised at once, without retries, so the caller's own retry loop can restart the whole transaction.
  • Pooled checkpointers retry when psycopg reports the connection broken, even when the error text is unfamiliar. This fixed checkpointer retries over TLS: on CockroachDB Cloud a dropped connection reads "SSL error: unexpected eof while reading" (OpenSSL 3), which was not recognized, so a pooled saver gave up instead of retrying. That wording is now also in TRANSIENT_MESSAGES. A definite SQLSTATE still decides first, as on the SQLAlchemy path.
  • AsyncCockroachDBSaver's sync methods raise a clear RuntimeError instead of hanging when the saver's loop is closed, stopped, or the process forked, and they cancel the abandoned work. put and put_writes called from the saver's own loop thread now raise InvalidStateError instead of deadlocking (the other sync methods already did).
  • Engines built with loop= (CockroachDBEngine(engine, loop=...) or CockroachDBEngine.from_engine(engine, loop=...)) fail fast with a clear RuntimeError instead of hanging when that loop is closed, never started, stops or closes during a call, or the process forked (including an engine rebuilt in a child around the parent's loop). A loop that has not started yet gets a short grace period (LOOP_START_TIMEOUT, 1 s).
  • RetryPolicy rejects NaN and infinity in its numeric fields, and delay() can no longer overflow for large attempt numbers or multipliers.
  • The flat jitter / retry_jitter argument now raises TypeError for anything other than True, False, 0 or 1. It used to be read by truthiness, so 0.3 became a jitter of 0.5. Use RetryPolicy(jitter=...) for a ratio.
  • Retry warnings name the underlying driver error when an application wraps it, and never include SQL text or parameter values.
  • aadd_texts, add_texts, afrom_texts and from_texts validate input (lengths, ids, duplicates, metadata JSON and batch_size) before calling the embedding model, so invalid input no longer pays for embedding calls. The namespace conflict check is a database query and still runs after embedding.
  • Applying a vector index whose name already exists with different prefix columns (order or count) or a different partition size you set now logs a WARNING naming each difference, like the existing opclass warning, instead of doing nothing silently. Applying the same index again logs nothing. A partition size you leave unset accepts whatever the index has.
  • Checkpointer setup logs its bootstrap step as "checkpointer setup" instead of a second "checkpointer migration 0".

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• RetryPolicy: one configurable object for which errors are retried and how, set on the engine and inherited by the vector store and chat history; checkpointers take one too. Exported defaults (RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES, TRANSIENT_MESSAGES, ...) and get_sqlstate().
  • Retries for 40001, 40003, every 08xxx code, 57P01, 58C00, 58C01 and 53300, plus connection loss reported without a code. Failed logins and SSL or configuration errors are never retried.
  • Optional hang guard (attempt_timeout, ddl_attempt_timeout) that abandons and retries an attempt the server never answers.
  • aadd_embeddings/add_embeddings, amax_marginal_relevance_search_by_vector, the full langchain-postgres filter grammar ($between, $exists, $like, $ilike, $not).
  • CockroachDBChatMessageHistory accepts a shared CockroachDBEngine and has a public acreate_table_if_not_exists().
  • Checkpointer from_conn_string options: retry_policy, connect_timeout, prepare_threshold, connect_kwargs.
  • connect_timeout on CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string (default 10 seconds).
  • CockroachDBEngine.from_engine(engine, loop=...).
  • postgresql:// and cockroachdb:// URL spellings are normalized to the psycopg driver.
  • examples/resilience.py, end-to-end tests for every example, LangGraph checkpointer conformance tests, and integration tests that inject real CockroachDB faults.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Errors were classified by psycopg2's pgcode, which psycopg 3 does not set, and by words like "connection" and "timeout" in any exception. Missing tables and statement timeouts were retried.
  • The vector store never applied its retry settings; chat history and both checkpointers had no retries.
  • Sync methods failed under concurrency ("bound to a different event loop") because every call ran its own event loop against a shared pool. They now share one background loop.
  • Metadata filters broke on apostrophes, could carry injected SQL, and failed on boolean and null values. All values are bound parameters now.
  • Vector indexes ignored the distance strategy and were always vector_l2_ops, so cosine and inner product searches never used them.
  • vector_search_beam_size stayed set on pooled connections after a search.
  • Chat history add_messages could leave partial writes and could duplicate messages on retry.
  • MMR re-embedded every candidate through the embeddings API.
  • from_texts failed with ids or vector store arguments.
  • Concurrent checkpointer setup() could fail on a duplicate migration version, and calling the saver while iterating list() deadlocked.
  • Running setup a second time failed with SQLSTATE 57000 when autocommit_before_ddl was off and the table was schema_locked, which is the default for new tables on v26. This hit init_vectorstore_table with namespace_column or create_tsvector, and chat history create_table_if_not_exists. Schema setup now runs one statement per implicit transaction.
  • In pipeline mode, checkpointer setup() and enable_ttl()/disable_ttl() failed with autocommit_before_ddl off. That covered a fresh database and an upgrade that adds migrations. Every schema statement now runs in its own implicit transaction.
  • After a session is canceled (CANCEL SESSION, or a connection dropped by a load balancer or drain), CockroachDB can answer the next query with SQLSTATE XXUUU "read tcp ...: i/o timeout". v25.4 always does; v26.3 sometimes does. The checkpointers raised it. It is now retried on a fresh connection.
  • In a vector store with a namespace, adding a document whose id already belonged to another namespace overwrote that row and moved it into the writing namespace. Such ids now raise ValueError before anything is written, and the upsert never updates a row in another namespace.
  • New connections set gssencmode=disable unless the URL or connect args choose otherwise. CockroachDB has no GSS encryption, and this avoids a Kerberos lookup that can crash forked workers on macOS.
  • adrop_vector_index() and drop_vector_index() can be called without an index to drop the default-named index, as the upgrade note says.
  • from_texts(namespace=...) now creates the namespace column.
  • Two spellings of the same UUID in one call are rejected as duplicates.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• psycopg 3 only: psycopg2-binary is no longer a dependency. Requires langchain-core 1.x and caps every dependency at its next major version. Python 3.10 to 3.14.
  • Supports CockroachDB v25.4 or later; tested on v25.4 LTS and v26.3.
  • The vector store's retry settings default to the engine's (5 attempts) instead of 3.
  • max_retries < 1 raises ValueError instead of never calling the function.
  • Table, schema, column and index names must be plain SQL identifiers.
  • Indexes created by 0.3.x for COSINE or INNER_PRODUCT should be dropped and applied again.
  • add_texts/add_embeddings reject duplicate ids within one call (ValueError), and metadata that is not JSON serializable, including NaN and infinity (TypeError). Both checks run before anything is written. They used to fail partway, after earlier batches had committed.
  • Range filters ($gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $between) with a string value now compare as text, and only match string fields, like langchain-postgres. In 0.3.0, {"year": {"$gte": "2020"}} matched numeric fields; pass a number to compare numerically.
  • Top-level keys next to $and/$or used to be ignored. They are now combined with AND, so results can narrow.
  • The retry_* attributes on the engine and vector store are now read-only properties. Set them through retry_policy or the constructor.
  • Chat message ids are generated by the client before the first attempt.
  • batch_size is capped at 16,383. Long id lists are split automatically.

docs.title: langchain_cockroachdb.checkpointer.saver.CockroachDBSaver
docs.text:
Bases: PsycopgOps, BaseCockroachDBSaver

Synchronous checkpointer that stores checkpoints in CockroachDB.

Uses raw psycopg3 connections (not SQLAlchemy) for compatibility with LangGraph's checkpointer interface. For production, pass a psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool: it replaces broken connections, while a single connection cannot recover from a dropped connection.

On a pool, operations run concurrently, each on its own pooled connection. On a single connection they run one at a time. A write with several statements runs them in one transaction, so it is saved completely or not at all, even when the caller stops partway through. On a single connection the caller also uses, an operation inside a transaction the caller opened joins that transaction, and its errors are raised at once, not retried, so the caller can retry the whole transaction.

Example 
from psycopg.rows import dict_row
from psycopg_pool import ConnectionPool
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver, RetryPolicy

pool = ConnectionPool(
    "postgresql://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable",
    kwargs={"autocommit": True, "row_factory": dict_row},
    open=True,
)
checkpointer = CockroachDBSaver(pool, retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=8))
checkpointer.setup()
graph = workflow.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

docs.title: disable_ttl()
docs.text:
Disable CockroachDB row-level TTL on checkpoint tables.

Safe to run from several processes at once. On CockroachDB v25.4 a TTL change fails while another one runs on the same table; that error is retried with the budget that schema_change_policy gives it, up to ten minutes by default, even if the policy's retry_on would refuse it. max_attempts=1 turns this off. Other savers see the change within TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS.

docs.title: enable_ttl(ttl_interval='7 days', cron='@daily')
docs.text:
Enable CockroachDB row-level TTL on checkpoint tables.

Rows older than ttl_interval will be automatically deleted by a background CockroachDB job on the specified cron schedule. Blob rows, which hold channel values, expire a tenth of ttl_interval later (TTL_REFRESH_FRACTION), and each put brings forward those its checkpoint still uses. So a thread keeps its state while it is active, and expires once it has been idle for ttl_interval. Months and years are stored as days, 30 to a month and 365 to a year, so the interval has a fixed length.

When the TTL setting of checkpoint_blobs is to change, it writes the new settings with TTL paused, so nothing is deleted, and waits TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS plus TTL_PAUSE_MARGIN_SECONDS, or plus the retry policy's attempt_timeout when that is longer, so that every saver reads them and refreshes on its puts, and puts already under way finish; savers refresh while TTL is paused. Then it makes one pass, so threads idle at that moment keep their state too: each blob row that checkpoints inside the interval use, and that is older than the newest of them by more than the refresh window, is brought forward to now. Only rows left unchanged that long are rewritten. The pass reads every checkpoint once, TTL_REFRESH_BATCH_SIZE at a time, changes at most TTL_REFRESH_UPDATE_SIZE rows per UPDATE, and logs at INFO when it starts and ends. Then it reads the setting again and resumes TTL, unless another run has written a different setting since: that run resumes it, and this one logs at INFO. So it blocks for about 15 seconds by default, plus the pass, whenever the setting changes, on a table of any size. With the same setting in place and running, it only updates the cron and returns at once; any other change makes the whole run, a longer interval too. A run that stops partway leaves TTL paused, on checkpoint_blobs at least, and the next run finishes it, even with the same arguments; to force a pass, call disable_ttl first. If startup probes are tight, run it once from a single process or a one-off job before a rollout. Use one interval, and change it from one process. After upgrading from 0.5, run it again with the same arguments, which adds the grace and covers threads idle since the upgrade. Intervals over 106,751 days, the longest duration CockroachDB keeps, are refused.

Safe to run from several processes at once. On CockroachDB v25.4 a TTL change fails while another one runs on the same table; that error is retried with the budget that schema_change_policy gives it, up to ten minutes by default, even if the policy's retry_on would refuse it. max_attempts=1 turns this off. Other savers see the change within TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ttl_interval str

Interval after which rows expire (e.g., '7 days', '30 days').

'7 days' cron str

Cron schedule for the TTL deletion job (default: '@daily').

'@daily'

docs.text: Asynchronous checkpointer for LangGraph workflows.

docs.title: langchain_cockroachdb.checkpointer.async_saver.AsyncCockroachDBSaver
docs.text:
Bases: AsyncPsycopgOps, BaseCockroachDBSaver

Asynchronous checkpointer that stores checkpoints in CockroachDB.

Uses raw psycopg3 async connections (not SQLAlchemy) for compatibility with LangGraph's checkpointer interface. For production, pass a psycopg_pool.AsyncConnectionPool: it replaces broken connections, while a single connection cannot recover from a dropped connection.

On a pool, operations run concurrently, each on its own pooled connection. On a single connection they run one at a time. A write with several statements runs them in one transaction, so it is saved completely or not at all, even when the caller is cancelled partway through. On a single connection the caller also uses, an operation inside a transaction the caller opened joins that transaction, and its errors are raised at once, not retried, so the caller can retry the whole transaction.

The sync methods (get_tuple, put and the others) run the async ones on the event loop the saver was created on, so call them from other threads while that loop runs. From the loop itself they raise asyncio.InvalidStateError. When the loop is closed or stops, or in a forked child, they raise RuntimeError instead of waiting forever.

Example 
from psycopg.rows import dict_row
from psycopg_pool import AsyncConnectionPool
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBSaver, RetryPolicy

async with AsyncConnectionPool(
    "postgresql://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable",
    kwargs={"autocommit": True, "row_factory": dict_row},
) as pool:
    checkpointer = AsyncCockroachDBSaver(pool, retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=8))
    await checkpointer.setup()
    graph = workflow.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

Rows older than ttl_interval will be automatically deleted by a background CockroachDB job on the specified cron schedule. Blob rows, which hold channel values, expire a tenth of ttl_interval later (TTL_REFRESH_FRACTION), and each put brings forward those its checkpoint still uses. So a thread keeps its state while it is active, and expires once it has been idle for ttl_interval. Months and years are stored as days, 30 to a month and 365 to a year, so the interval has a fixed length.

When the TTL setting of checkpoint_blobs is to change, it writes the new settings with TTL paused, so nothing is deleted, and waits TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS plus TTL_PAUSE_MARGIN_SECONDS, or plus the retry policy's attempt_timeout when that is longer, so that every saver reads them and refreshes on its puts, and puts already under way finish; savers refresh while TTL is paused. Then it makes one pass, so threads idle at that moment keep their state too: each blob row that checkpoints inside the interval use, and that is older than the newest of them by more than the refresh window, is brought forward to now. Only rows left unchanged that long are rewritten. The pass reads every checkpoint once, TTL_REFRESH_BATCH_SIZE at a time, changes at most TTL_REFRESH_UPDATE_SIZE rows per UPDATE, and logs at INFO when it starts and ends. Then it reads the setting again and resumes TTL, unless another run has written a different setting since: that run resumes it, and this one logs at INFO. So it blocks for about 15 seconds by default, plus the pass, whenever the setting changes, on a table of any size. With the same setting in place and running, it only updates the cron and returns at once; any other change makes the whole run, a longer interval too. A run that stops partway leaves TTL paused, on checkpoint_blobs at least, and the next run finishes it, even with the same arguments; to force a pass, call disable_ttl first. If startup probes are tight, run it once from a single process or a one-off job before a rollout. Use one interval, and change it from one process. After upgrading from 0.5, run it again with the same arguments, which adds the grace and covers threads idle since the upgrade. Intervals over 106,751 days, the longest duration CockroachDB keeps, are refused.

Safe to run from several processes at once. On CockroachDB v25.4 a TTL change fails while another one runs on the same table; that error is retried with the budget that schema_change_policy gives it, up to ten minutes by default, even if the policy's retry_on would refuse it. max_attempts=1 turns this off. Other savers see the change within TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ttl_interval str

Interval after which rows expire (e.g., '7 days', '30 days').

'7 days' cron str

Cron schedule for the TTL deletion job (default: '@daily').

'@daily'

docs.title: langchain_cockroachdb.retry
docs.text:
Retry policy for CockroachDB operations.

CockroachDB runs transactions at SERIALIZABLE isolation by default, so clients are expected to retry some errors. This module decides which errors are worth retrying and runs operations with exponential backoff and jitter.

A 40001 error means the transaction did not commit, so retrying it is always safe. After 40003 (result is ambiguous) or a lost connection the transaction may have committed, so only idempotent work should be retried. Every write this package issues is idempotent (UPSERT, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, DELETE, IF [NOT] EXISTS).

docs.title: RetryPolicy dataclass
docs.text:
Which CockroachDB errors to retry, and how.

Every field can be changed. RetryPolicy(**mapping) accepts plain lists for the code and phrase fields, so policies can come from YAML or environment variables. Use dataclasses.replace to derive a policy.

Attributes:

Name Type Description max_attempts int

Total attempts, including the first (default: 5)

initial_backoff float

Delay before the first retry, in seconds (default: 0.1)

max_backoff float

Upper bound for any delay, in seconds (default: 10.0)

backoff_multiplier float

Growth factor between delays (default: 2.0)

jitter float

Fraction of each delay that is randomized, 0 to 1 (default: 0.5)

retryable_sqlstates frozenset[str]

SQLSTATEs to retry (default: RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES)

retryable_sqlstate_classes frozenset[str]

Two-character SQLSTATE classes to retry (default: RETRYABLE_SQLSTATE_CLASSES)

uncategorized_sqlstates frozenset[str]

Codes too generic to decide on; message phrases decide instead (default: UNCATEGORIZED_SQLSTATES)

transient_messages tuple[str, ...]

Phrases that mark an error without a usable code as transient (default: TRANSIENT_MESSAGES)

non_transient_messages tuple[str, ...]

Phrases that rule out a retry for errors without a usable code (default: NON_TRANSIENT_MESSAGES)

retry_on Callable[[BaseException], bool] | None

Custom predicate that replaces the rules above

attempt_timeout float | None

Seconds before a hung query or write is abandoned and retried; None disables the guard (default: None)

ddl_attempt_timeout float | None

Same guard, bounds each schema change (default: None)

Example 
# Ride through multi-region failovers: also retry statement timeouts
# and cut off attempts that hang for more than 10 seconds.
policy = RetryPolicy(
    retryable_sqlstates=RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES | {"57014"},
    attempt_timeout=10,
)
Source code in langchain_cockroachdb/retry.py 
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RetryPolicy:
    """Which CockroachDB errors to retry, and how.

    Every field can be changed. ``RetryPolicy(**mapping)`` accepts plain lists
    for the code and phrase fields, so policies can come from YAML or
    environment variables. Use ``dataclasses.replace`` to derive a policy.

    Attributes:
        max_attempts: Total attempts, including the first (default: 5)
        initial_backoff: Delay before the first retry, in seconds (default: 0.1)
        max_backoff: Upper bound for any delay, in seconds (default: 10.0)
        backoff_multiplier: Growth factor between delays (default: 2.0)
        jitter: Fraction of each delay that is randomized, 0 to 1 (default: 0.5)
        retryable_sqlstates: SQLSTATEs to retry (default: RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES)
        retryable_sqlstate_classes: Two-character SQLSTATE classes to retry
            (default: RETRYABLE_SQLSTATE_CLASSES)
        uncategorized_sqlstates: Codes too generic to decide on; message
            phrases decide instead (default: UNCATEGORIZED_SQLSTATES)
        transient_messages: Phrases that mark an error without a usable code
            as transient (default: TRANSIENT_MESSAGES)
        non_transient_messages: Phrases that rule out a retry for errors
            without a usable code (default: NON_TRANSIENT_MESSAGES)
        retry_on: Custom predicate that replaces the rules above
        attempt_timeout: Seconds before a hung query or write is abandoned and
            retried; None disables the guard (default: None)
        ddl_attempt_timeout: Same guard, bounds each schema change (default: None)

    Example:
        ```python
        # Ride through multi-region failovers: also retry statement timeouts
        # and cut off attempts that hang for more than 10 seconds.
        policy = RetryPolicy(
            retryable_sqlstates=RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES | {"57014"},
            attempt_timeout=10,
        )
        ```
    """

    max_attempts: int = 5
    initial_backoff: float = 0.1
    max_backoff: float = 10.0
    backoff_multiplier: float = 2.0
    jitter: float = 0.5
    retryable_sqlstates: frozenset[str] = RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES
    retryable_sqlstate_classes: frozenset[str] = RETRYABLE_SQLSTATE_CLASSES
    uncategorized_sqlstates: frozenset[str] = UNCATEGORIZED_SQLSTATES
    transient_messages: tuple[str, ...] = TRANSIENT_MESSAGES
    non_transient_messages: tuple[str, ...] = NON_TRANSIENT_MESSAGES
    retry_on: Callable[[BaseException], bool] | None = None
    attempt_timeout: float | None = None
    ddl_attempt_timeout: float | None = None

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        self._validate_max_attempts()
        self._validate_numeric_fields()
        self._validate_timeouts()
        self._normalize_collections()

    def _validate_max_attempts(self) -> None:
        if (
            isinstance(self.max_attempts, bool)
            or not isinstance(self.max_attempts, int)
            or self.max_attempts < 1
        ):
            raise ValueError("max_attempts must be an integer of at least 1")

    def _validate_numeric_fields(self) -> None:
        for name in ("initial_backoff", "max_backoff", "backoff_multiplier", "jitter"):
            value = getattr(self, name)
            if not math.isfinite(value):
                raise ValueError(f"{name} must be finite, not NaN or infinity")
        if self.initial_backoff < 0:
            raise ValueError("initial_backoff must not be negative")
        if self.max_backoff < self.initial_backoff:
            raise ValueError("max_backoff must be at least initial_backoff")
        if self.backoff_multiplier < 1:
            raise ValueError("backoff_multiplier must be at least 1")
        if isinstance(self.jitter, bool):
            raise TypeError("jitter is a ratio from 0 to 1, for example 0.5 or 0")
        if not 0 <= self.jitter <= 1:
            raise ValueError("jitter must be between 0 and 1")

    def _validate_timeouts(self) -> None:
        for name in ("attempt_timeout", "ddl_attempt_timeout"):
            value = getattr(self, name)
            if value is not None:
                if not math.isfinite(value):
                    raise ValueError(f"{name} must be finite, not NaN or infinity")
                if value <= 0:
                    raise ValueError(f"{name} must be positive or None")

    def _normalize_collections(self) -> None:
        for name in (
            "retryable_sqlstates",
            "retryable_sqlstate_classes",
            "uncategorized_sqlstates",
        ):
            object.__setattr__(self, name, _as_codes(getattr(self, name), name))
        for name in ("transient_messages", "non_transient_messages"):
            object.__setattr__(self, name, _as_phrases(getattr(self, name), name))

    def is_retryable(self, error: BaseException) -> bool:
        """Return True if ``error`` is worth retrying under this policy."""
        if self.retry_on is not None:
            return bool(self.retry_on(error))
        code = get_sqlstate(error)
        if code is not None:
            if code in self.retryable_sqlstates or code[:2] in self.retryable_sqlstate_classes:
                return True
            if code not in self.uncategorized_sqlstates:
                return False
        chain = list(_error_chain(error))
        if not any(isinstance(e, _driver_error_types()) for e in chain):
            return False
        if any(isinstance(e, (PoolTimeout, PoolCheckoutTimeout)) for e in chain):
            return False
        # SQLAlchemy embeds the statement and its parameters in str(StatementError)
        # and str(DBAPIError), which can hold user data, so only driver and
        # application messages count for phrase matching.
        messages = [str(e).lower() for e in chain if not isinstance(e, StatementError)]
        if any(phrase in m for m in messages for phrase in self.non_transient_messages):
            return False
        # SQLAlchemy sets this after it discards a connection that broke. The
        # checkpointers set it when psycopg reports a pooled connection broken.
        if any(getattr(e, "connection_invalidated", False) for e in chain):
            return True
        return any(phrase in m for m in messages for phrase in self.transient_messages)

    def delay(self, retry_number: int, *, rand: Callable[[], float] = random.random) -> float:
        """Seconds to wait before retry ``retry_number`` (0 for the first retry)."""
        exponent = min(max(retry_number, 0), 64)
        try:
            base = min(self.initial_backoff * self.backoff_multiplier**exponent, self.max_backoff)
        except OverflowError:
            base = self.max_backoff
        return base * (1 - self.jitter * rand())

    def run(
        self,
        fn: Callable[[], T],
        *,
        label: str = "operation",
        can_retry: Callable[[BaseException], bool] | None = None,
        sleep: Callable[[float], Any] = time.sleep,
    ) -> T:
        """Call ``fn`` until it succeeds or fails with an error not worth retrying.

        Args:
            fn: The attempt; called again from scratch on every retry
            label: What the attempt does, used in log messages
            can_retry: Extra check; when it returns False the error is raised
            sleep: Sleep function (tests pass a fake)

        Returns:
            Whatever ``fn`` returns
        """
        state = _RunState()
        while True:
            try:
                return fn()
            except Exception as error:
                pause = self._pause_before_retry(error, state, label, can_retry)
                if pause is None:
                    raise
                sleep(pause)

    async def arun(
        self,
        fn: Callable[[], Awaitable[T]],
        *,
        label: str = "operation",
        can_retry: Callable[[BaseException], bool] | None = None,
        sleep: Callable[[float], Awaitable[Any]] = asyncio.sleep,
    ) -> T:
        """Async version of :meth:`run`; ``fn`` returns a new awaitable per attempt."""
        state = _RunState()
        while True:
            try:
                return await fn()
            except Exception as error:
                pause = self._pause_before_retry(error, state, label, can_retry)
                if pause is None:
                    raise
                await sleep(pause)

    def _pause_before_retry(
        self,
        error: BaseException,
        state: _RunState,
        label: str,
        can_retry: Callable[[BaseException], bool] | None,
    ) -> float | None:
        """Seconds to wait before the next attempt after ``error``, or None to raise it."""
        attempt = state.failed = state.failed + 1
        if not self._should_retry(error, attempt, label, can_retry):
            return None
        pause = self.delay(attempt - 1)
        self._log_retry(error, attempt, pause, label)
        return pause

    def _should_retry(
        self,
        error: BaseException,
        attempt: int,
        label: str,
        can_retry: Callable[[BaseException], bool] | None,
    ) -> bool:
        if not self.is_retryable(error):
            return False
        if can_retry is not None and not can_retry(error):
            return False
        if attempt >= self.max_attempts:
            logger.warning(
                "Giving up on %s after %d attempts: %s", label, attempt, _describe(error)
            )
            return False
        return True

    def _log_retry(self, error: BaseException, attempt: int, pause: float, label: str) -> None:
        logger.warning(
            "Retrying %s after %s (attempt %d of %d failed, next try in %.2fs)",
            label,
            _describe(error),
            attempt,
            self.max_attempts,
            pause,
        )

def delay(self, retry_number: int, *, rand: Callable[[], float] = random.random) -> float:
    """Seconds to wait before retry ``retry_number`` (0 for the first retry)."""
    exponent = min(max(retry_number, 0), 64)
    try:
        base = min(self.initial_backoff * self.backoff_multiplier**exponent, self.max_backoff)
    except OverflowError:
        base = self.max_backoff
    return base * (1 - self.jitter * rand())

def is_retryable(self, error: BaseException) -> bool:
    """Return True if ``error`` is worth retrying under this policy."""
    if self.retry_on is not None:
        return bool(self.retry_on(error))
    code = get_sqlstate(error)
    if code is not None:
        if code in self.retryable_sqlstates or code[:2] in self.retryable_sqlstate_classes:
            return True
        if code not in self.uncategorized_sqlstates:
            return False
    chain = list(_error_chain(error))
    if not any(isinstance(e, _driver_error_types()) for e in chain):
        return False
    if any(isinstance(e, (PoolTimeout, PoolCheckoutTimeout)) for e in chain):
        return False
    # SQLAlchemy embeds the statement and its parameters in str(StatementError)
    # and str(DBAPIError), which can hold user data, so only driver and
    # application messages count for phrase matching.
    messages = [str(e).lower() for e in chain if not isinstance(e, StatementError)]
    if any(phrase in m for m in messages for phrase in self.non_transient_messages):
        return False
    # SQLAlchemy sets this after it discards a connection that broke. The
    # checkpointers set it when psycopg reports a pooled connection broken.
    if any(getattr(e, "connection_invalidated", False) for e in chain):
        return True
    return any(phrase in m for m in messages for phrase in self.transient_messages)

def async_retry_with_backoff(
    max_retries: int | None = None,
    initial_backoff: float | None = None,
    max_backoff: float | None = None,
    backoff_multiplier: float | None = None,
    jitter: bool | None = None,
    *,
    retry_on: Callable[[BaseException], bool] | None = None,
    policy: RetryPolicy | None = None,
) -> Callable[[Callable[..., Awaitable[T]]], Callable[..., Awaitable[T]]]:
    """Retry an async function on transient CockroachDB errors.

    Unset arguments fall back to ``RetryPolicy`` defaults (5 attempts, 0.1s
    initial backoff, 10s cap, doubling, jitter on). The whole function runs
    again on each attempt, so it should open its own transaction.

    After 40003 or a lost connection the work may already have committed:
    only decorate idempotent work, or pass
    ``retry_on=lambda e: get_sqlstate(e) == "40001"``.

    Args:
        max_retries: Total attempts, including the first
        initial_backoff: Delay before the first retry, in seconds
        max_backoff: Upper bound for any delay, in seconds
        backoff_multiplier: Growth factor between delays
        jitter: Randomize delays (True maps to a 0.5 ratio)
        retry_on: Custom predicate deciding which errors to retry
        policy: A complete RetryPolicy, instead of the arguments above

    Example:
        ```python
        @async_retry_with_backoff(max_retries=3)
        async def upsert(conn):
            await conn.execute(text("UPSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'a')"))
        ```
    """
    resolved = _decorator_policy(
        max_retries, initial_backoff, max_backoff, backoff_multiplier, jitter, retry_on, policy
    )

    def decorator(func: Callable[..., Awaitable[T]]) -> Callable[..., Awaitable[T]]:
        label = getattr(func, "__qualname__", None) or getattr(func, "__name__", None) or repr(func)

        @functools.wraps(func)
        async def wrapper(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> T:
            return await resolved.arun(lambda: func(*args, **kwargs), label=label)

        return wrapper

    return decorator

def get_sqlstate(error: BaseException) -> str | None:
    """Return the SQLSTATE carried by an error or by anything that caused it.

    Reads ``sqlstate`` (psycopg 3, asyncpg) and ``pgcode`` (psycopg2), looking
    through SQLAlchemy's wrapped ``orig`` and ``raise ... from`` causes.

    Args:
        error: The exception to inspect

    Returns:
        The five-character SQLSTATE, or None if nothing in the chain has one
    """
    for current in _error_chain(error):
        for attr in ("sqlstate", "pgcode"):
            code = getattr(current, attr, None)
            if isinstance(code, str) and len(code) == 5:
                return code.upper()
    return None

def is_schema_change_busy(
    error: BaseException, messages: Iterable[str] = SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_MESSAGES
) -> bool:
    """True if ``error`` says another schema change on the table is still running.

    The error must carry SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_SQLSTATE and one of ``messages``

    if get_sqlstate(error) != SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_SQLSTATE:
        return False
    phrases = _as_phrases(messages, "messages")
    return any(
        phrase in str(current).lower() for current in _error_chain(error) for phrase in phrases

def may_have_committed(error: BaseException) -> bool:
    """Whether a transaction that sent its COMMIT, then failed with ``error``, may have committed.

    Only a definite abort, an error whose SQLSTATE is in
    DEFINITE_ABORT_SQLSTATES, proves that it did not. A 40003, a lost
    connection, an attempt the hang guard abandoned and every other error
    leave the outcome unknown, so they count as may have committed.

    Args:
        error: The exception that ended the transaction's attempt

    Returns:
        False only for a definite abort
    """
    return get_sqlstate(error) not in DEFINITE_ABORT_SQLSTATES

def resolve_retry_policy(
    policy: RetryPolicy | None,
    *,
    base: RetryPolicy,
    max_attempts: int | None = None,
    initial_backoff: float | None = None,
    max_backoff: float | None = None,
    backoff_multiplier: float | None = None,
    jitter: bool | None = None,
    jitter_name: str = "retry_jitter",
) -> RetryPolicy:
    """Combine an explicit policy, or flat ``retry_*`` arguments, with a base policy.

    ``jitter`` is an on or off switch: True or 1 means a ratio of 0.5, False
    or 0 means none. ``jitter_name`` is the argument's name in error messages.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If both a policy and flat arguments are given
        TypeError: If jitter is not None, True, False, 0 or 1
    """
    # The ints 0 and 1 are accepted so callers who passed them keep working
    if jitter is not None and not (
        isinstance(jitter, bool) or (type(jitter) is int and jitter in (0, 1))
    ):
        raise TypeError(
            f"{jitter_name} must be True, False, 0 or 1, not {jitter!r}; "
            "for a ratio, use RetryPolicy(jitter=...)"
        )
    overrides: dict[str, Any] = {
        "max_attempts": max_attempts,
        "initial_backoff": initial_backoff,
        "max_backoff": max_backoff,
        "backoff_multiplier": backoff_multiplier,
        "jitter": None if jitter is None else (0.5 if jitter else 0.0),
    }
    overrides = {name: value for name, value in overrides.items() if value is not None}
    if policy is not None:
        if overrides:
            raise ValueError("Pass either retry_policy or retry_* arguments, not both")
        return policy
    return dataclasses.replace(base, **overrides) if overrides else base

docs.text:
policy, also retrying a schema change that met another running one.

For idempotent schema changes, such as TTL settings, that several processes may run at once. The busy error (see is_schema_change_busy) is retried even when the policy's own retry_on would return False for it. It means waiting for the other schema change to finish, such as a column backfill or a vector index build, which takes far longer than a transient error takes to clear. So it has a budget of its own: it is retried for up to seconds of wall time from the first busy error (default SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_SECONDS, ten minutes, as long as the store's setup() waits for another process's migration). The pauses grow as the policy's backoff does, from RetryPolicy's default initial backoff when the policy has none, at least doubling, up to max_backoff seconds (default SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_MAX_BACKOFF), or up to the initial backoff if that is larger. seconds=0 turns this off. It logs a WARNING on the first retry, then at most one every SCHEMA_CHANGE_PROGRESS_SECONDS, and one when it gives up.

Every other error is decided by policy itself, including its retry_on, attempts and backoff, and a subclass's overrides of is_retryable and delay. Overrides of run and arun are not kept. Those attempts are counted apart from the busy error's. Timeouts are the policy's, and max_attempts=1 turns every retry off. A policy derived from the result with dataclasses.replace keeps both together.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If seconds or max_backoff is negative or not finite

    policy: RetryPolicy,
    messages: Iterable[str] = SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_MESSAGES,
    *,
    seconds: float = SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_SECONDS,
    max_backoff: float = SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_MAX_BACKOFF,
) -> RetryPolicy:
    """``policy``, also retrying a schema change that met another running one.

    For idempotent schema changes, such as TTL settings, that several
    processes may run at once. The busy error (see is_schema_change_busy)
    is retried even when the policy's own ``retry_on`` would return False
    for it. It means waiting for the other schema change to finish, such as
    a column backfill or a vector index build, which takes far longer than
    a transient error takes to clear. So it has a budget of its own: it is
    retried for up to ``seconds`` of wall time from the first busy error
    (default SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_SECONDS, ten minutes, as long as the
    store's setup() waits for another process's migration). The pauses
    grow as the policy's backoff does, from RetryPolicy's default initial
    backoff when the policy has none, at least doubling, up to
    ``max_backoff`` seconds (default SCHEMA_CHANGE_BUSY_MAX_BACKOFF), or up
    to the initial backoff if that is larger. ``seconds=0`` turns this off.
    It logs a WARNING on the first retry, then at most one every
    SCHEMA_CHANGE_PROGRESS_SECONDS, and one when it gives up.

    Every other error is decided by ``policy`` itself, including its
    ``retry_on``, attempts and backoff, and a subclass's overrides of
    is_retryable and delay. Overrides of run and arun are not kept. Those
    attempts are counted apart from the busy error's. Timeouts are the
    policy's, and ``max_attempts=1`` turns every retry off. A policy
    derived from the result with dataclasses.replace keeps both together.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If ``seconds`` or ``max_backoff`` is negative or not
            finite
    """
    phrases = _as_phrases(messages, "messages")
    fields = {field.name: getattr(policy, field.name) for field in dataclasses.fields(RetryPolicy)}
    return _SchemaChangePolicy(
        **fields,
        base=policy,
        busy_messages=phrases,
        busy_seconds=seconds,
        busy_max_backoff=max_backoff,
    )

docs.title: langchain_cockroachdb.store.store.CockroachDBStore
docs.text:
Bases: BaseStore, BaseCockroachDBStore, PsycopgOps

LangGraph store that keeps long-term memory in CockroachDB.

Items live in one table keyed by namespace and key. Namespaces are stored as their labels joined with ".". For production, pass a psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool or use from_conn_string with pool_config: a pool replaces broken connections and runs batches concurrently, while a single connection runs one batch at a time.

A batch runs its reads first, then all its puts and deletes in one transaction. Its gets, its searches and its listings take one round trip each. On a store with a vector index, semantic searches under a namespace add one before the searches, to find their namespaces, and one after them when a search must run again exactly. A flat store adds neither. The long-term memory guide explains why.

With history, a batch that overwrites or deletes a memory first copies the version it ends into a history table, in its transaction. delete then keeps the memory in history; purge removes a memory with its history, and history lists the old versions.

Example 
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBStore

with CockroachDBStore.from_conn_string(
    "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"
) as store:
    store.setup()
    store.put(("users", "123"), "prefs", {"theme": "dark"})
    item = store.get(("users", "123"), "prefs")

docs.title: confirm(namespace, key, *, ttl=NOT_PROVIDED)
docs.text:
Mark a live memory as confirmed, renewing its expiry and counting confirmations.

This counts the confirmation and renews the expiry. That way expiry can follow how often a fact is confirmed, not how often it is read. Confirming does not change the version or updated_at, so it never invalidates a pending find_conflicts. Confirmations belong to the memory's value: a write that changes it starts them again from none.

Each call picks a confirmation id before its first attempt and stores it on the memory, so a retry after a commit whose result was lost counts nothing again, unless another confirmation of the same memory lands in between, in which case the retry counts again. The memory's write id stays as it is, so a write retried after its own lost commit still finds it.

docs.title: delete_if(namespace, key, *, expected)
docs.text:
Delete a memory only if it is still the one the caller read, in one transaction.

delete_if deletes only if the live memory under key still has the version and updated_at of expected, as put_if checks them. On a match it deletes as delete does: on a store with history the memory is kept in history as deleted, and its vectors go. With expected=None it applies only while no live memory has the key, so it deletes nothing live.

applied=True means the memory matched expected and this call deleted it, or, after an earlier attempt of the call that may have committed, that the memory is gone and was this call's to delete: it matched expected when that attempt checked it. On a mismatch it deletes nothing and returns applied=False with current, the live memory as the same transaction read it, or None if there is none, as when another writer deleted it or it expired since. A conflict is returned, not raised.

If an attempt sends its COMMIT and the result is lost, as when the connection drops while the COMMIT's answer travels, that attempt may have deleted the memory, so a retry that finds it gone reports it applied. On a store with history the retry also finds its own history row, which proves the earlier attempt deleted the memory, and the result has already_applied. A store without history keeps no row that proves which attempt deleted it, so already_applied stays False. Serialization failures and deadlocks (40001, 40P01) roll attempts back, so after only those a memory gone since is a conflict: another writer removed it. Once an attempt may have committed, the retries after it stay lenient, whatever error ends them next. If another writer put the key again before the retry, the retry reports a conflict with that memory.

docs.text:
Delete every item in a namespace and its descendants.

("user", "a") deletes ("user", "a") and ("user", "a", "b"), not ("user", "ab"). One statement deletes the items, their vectors and their history. A store without history deletes history too when the history table exists, as when the store kept history before, so nothing of the namespace is left. Its role then needs SELECT and DELETE on that table: without them the whole call fails with a permission error and deletes nothing, rather than forget only part of the namespace.
