docs.text:
Turn off CockroachDB row-level TTL on the store's tables.

Expired items are still left out of reads while omit_expired is on. Safe to run from several processes at once. On CockroachDB v25.4 a TTL change fails while another schema change runs on the same table; that error is retried with the budget that schema_change_policy gives it, up to ten minutes by default, even if the policy's retry_on would refuse it. max_attempts=1 turns this off.

docs.title: find_conflicts(namespace, key, value, *, slot=None, threshold=None, limit=10, filter=None, index=None, ttl=NOT_PROVIDED, provenance=None, valid_at=None)
docs.text:
Find the memories a new one may conflict with, without writing anything.

Candidates are live memories in namespace itself, not in its descendants, for one of three reasons, strongest first:

  • "key": the memory under key, whatever filter says.
  • "slot": with slot, the memories whose value holds the same value in that field, compared as JSON.
  • "similar": on a store with an index, the memories whose vectors score at or above threshold against the new memory's, with the store's score function: 1 minus the distance on a cosine store, the negated distance on an l2 or inner_product store. The new memory is embedded as a document (embed_documents), while search embeds its query (embed_query), so with a model that embeds the two differently the scores differ from search's.

Key and slot matches carry their best score when they have vectors, and similar ones always do. Candidates come strongest reason first, then best score, then key. Expired memories are never candidates, and no read pushes back an expiry.

The index fields of value are embedded once, and the embedding is kept for the write. Then two round trips read the candidates: first the database's clock, the key and slot matches and the namespace's vector count, then the similar memories and the scores. A namespace with at most reconcile_scan_limit vectors has all of them ranked. A larger one takes its similar candidates from a window of the C-SPANN index. When that window holds nothing below threshold and gave fewer than limit candidates, matches may lie beyond it, and one more round trip ranks every vector of the namespace.

None threshold float | None

docs.title: history(namespace, key=None, *, limit=20, offset=0)
docs.text:
The old versions of a memory, or of every memory in a namespace, newest first.

A store with history keeps every version that a write ends: one a put overwrites (reason "overwritten"), one a delete ends ("deleted"), and one that reconcile or resolve supersedes ("superseded", with superseded_by naming the memory that replaced it). A new memory that reconcile or resolve records as already superseded by a newer fact is kept there too, as "superseded". The live value is not one of them; get() returns it.

Without a key, it lists the old versions of every memory in exactly namespace, not its descendants, as get() reads a namespace. That is how to find the old versions of memories that reconcile saved under keys the store generated. Each version carries its own key and superseded_by, so versions can be grouped by a field of their value, or followed to the memory that replaced them. Each call reads the namespace's whole history to sort it, which suits per-user namespaces. For a very large history, page with limit and offset.

docs.title: put_if(namespace, key, value, *, expected, index=None, ttl=NOT_PROVIDED, provenance=None, valid_at=None)
docs.text:
Write a memory only if it is still the one the caller read, in one transaction.

Two threads that read the same memory with record() and both write it back with put would lose one update without a word. put_if writes only if the live memory under key still has the version and updated_at of expected, the check resolve makes: a put moves the version, and a 0.5.x store, which does not, still moves updated_at. With expected=None it writes only if no live memory has the key, so a memory is created once. An expired memory counts as absent.

On a match it writes as put does, in the transaction that checked: the write id goes on the row, the version it replaces is kept in history on a store with history, ending at valid_at when given or else at the write, and the memory's vectors are replaced. The result has applied set and the version written.

On a mismatch it writes nothing and returns applied=False with current, the live memory as the same transaction read it, or None if there is none. A conflict is an expected outcome here, so it is returned, not raised: merge and call put_if again with current, keep the stored memory, or ask the user.

The index fields of value are embedded once, before the first attempt. If an attempt commits and its result is lost, as when the connection drops while the COMMIT's answer travels, the retry finds the write id on the row and returns applied=True with already_applied. If another writer replaced the memory before the retry, a 0.5.x store included, the retry reports a conflict with that writer's memory, which is the current state.

docs.title: reconcile(namespace, key, value, *, policy, slot=None, threshold=None, limit=10, filter=None, index=None, ttl=NOT_PROVIDED, provenance=None, valid_at=None)
docs.text:
Write a memory and settle the memories it may conflict with, in one transaction.

The candidates are the ones find_conflicts finds: the live memory under key, the memories in the same slot and, on a store with an index, those that score at or above threshold. They are read in the transaction, policy decides what to do with the new memory and with each candidate, and the decision is applied before the transaction commits. Serializable isolation covers all of it: if another writer changes what the policy saw, one of the two transactions retries, and its policy sees the other's write. Two agents that reconcile contradicting memories for one user cannot both win.

policy runs inside the transaction, and runs again on every retry, so it must be a plain function, fast and deterministic: an async function is refused before any I/O. A slow policy holds the transaction open and can run past the attempt timeout. An LLM judge, or a person, belongs in find_conflicts and resolve, which hold no transaction while the decision is made. A policy must not call the store either: the store holds its connection while the policy runs, so such a call raises RuntimeError at once. A policy that raises rolls the transaction back, and its exception propagates unchanged, without a retry. So does the ValueError for an invalid decision.

The decision writes the new memory, as put does, with its provenance and valid time; skips it, as when it repeats a memory the decision confirms; or records it as superseded by a candidate whose fact is newer. A store with history records such a late fact straight into history; a store without history skips it. Each candidate is kept, superseded, deleted or confirmed. On a store with history, every version the decision ends is kept in history: the memory the new one overwrites and each candidate it supersedes end at the valid_at given, or at the write without one, and deleted ones end at the write. Without history, superseding and deleting remove the memory. Confirming sets confirmed_at, counts the confirmation and renews the memory's expiry from its own TTL. It changes neither the version nor updated_at.

The index fields of value are embedded once, before the first attempt. Each attempt reads the candidates in two round trips, as find_conflicts does, or three when the index's window may have left matches out. Then the policy runs, and the writes and the COMMIT go out together.

If an attempt commits and its result is lost, as when the connection drops while the COMMIT's answer travels, the retry finds the rows that carry its write id and writes nothing. It returns the result rebuilt from those rows, with already_applied set. That result lists only what the rows prove: kept is empty, and on a store without history so are superseded and deleted. A confirmation of the new memory in between leaves the write id on it. If another writer replaced the new memory before the retry, the history row of the version it overwrote, or of a memory it superseded, still proves the write: the result says it was written, with no version.

docs.title: resolve(conflicts, decision)
docs.text:
Apply a decision about what find_conflicts found, in one transaction.

This is the second step of the two-step flow: find_conflicts reads the candidates, an LLM or a person decides while no transaction is open, and resolve applies the decision as reconcile applies a policy's. It writes the new memory that find_conflicts planned, with its provenance, valid time and write id, and the vectors it embedded then, so nothing is embedded again. For the same reason it refuses a proposal edited after find_conflicts, rather than drop the edit: to change the memory, call find_conflicts again with the edited one.

In the same transaction, before it writes, resolve checks that nothing the decision depends on has changed. The memory under the new memory's key, and every candidate the decision supersedes, deletes or confirms, or names as superseding the new memory, must still have the version and updated_at that find_conflicts read. A memory written since counts as changed, also when a 0.5.x store wrote it, which sets updated_at without bumping the version. So does one deleted or expired since, and a live memory under the new key where find_conflicts found none. resolve then raises ConflictsChanged with those keys, writes nothing and does not retry: run find_conflicts again and decide again. Candidates the decision keeps are not checked, and confirming a memory changes neither its version nor updated_at, so a confirmation in between never counts.

The write id comes from find_conflicts. If a resolve of the same Conflicts already committed, as when an error left its outcome unknown and the caller calls again, resolve writes nothing and returns that write's result rebuilt from its rows, with already_applied set, whatever decision this call passes. As with reconcile, a rebuilt result lists only what the rows prove: kept is empty, and on a store without history so are superseded and deleted. Such a store keeps no row of a decision that only supersedes or deletes. When the commit of such a resolve is lost, its retry finds those memories gone, as the decision asked. So once an attempt of the call may have committed (it sent its COMMIT and failed with an error other than a serialization failure or a deadlock, which roll the attempt back), a memory the decision supersedes or deletes, the one under the new key included, counts as unchanged when it is gone. The retry applies the decision again, which changes nothing there, and returns its result without already_applied, since no row proves the earlier commit. After only serialization failures or deadlocks (40001, 40P01), which roll attempts back, the retry checks as strictly as the first attempt: a memory gone since was removed by another writer, and is a change. Once an attempt may have committed, the retries after it stay lenient, whatever error ends them next. A new call checks strictly again too: if an error escaped an earlier call, as when its retries ran out or the hang guard stopped it, and the caller calls resolve again, such a decision raises ConflictsChanged naming the keys that the earlier call removed. find_conflicts then shows the current state.

Without a valid_at given to find_conflicts, the new memory stores no valid time, so it is valid from its write, and the versions the decision ends end at that write. A Conflicts and a Decision can wait in a LangGraph checkpoint while a person decides: resolve takes them as the checkpoint gives them back.

docs.title: setup()
docs.text:
Create the store's tables and run its migrations.

MUST be called the first time the store is used. Safe to run from several processes at once: every migration is idempotent and versions are recorded with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. A setup() that finds another process still applying migration 2 waits for it, for up to SCHEMA_CHANGE_SETTLE_SECONDS, before it records the migration, so no store writes the new columns before they exist. When no job applies the migration, as after a peer's migration failed, it applies the migration itself. With an index, it creates the vectors table and its C-SPANN index (unless flat) on every call, then checks an existing index against the configuration. With history, it creates the history table, and with ttl_days turns on CockroachDB row-level TTL there. With a TTL configuration, it then turns on CockroachDB row-level TTL on expires_at.

It reads a table's TTL settings first and changes them only when they differ from the configuration. On CockroachDB v25.4 a TTL change fails while another schema change runs on the same table, such as a vector index that another setup() builds. That error is retried with the budget that schema_change_policy gives it, up to ten minutes by default for each table, even if the policy's retry_on would refuse it; max_attempts=1 turns this off.

An application role that did not run setup() needs SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the store's items and vectors tables, and on the history table when history is on. With history off, it still needs SELECT and DELETE on a history table that exists, left from when history was on, for delete_namespace. Without SELECT on the migrations table, or without a migrations table, as when the tables were created without setup(), the store finds migration 2 through the items table's columns instead. On a multi-node cluster, one write can then fail in the seconds after setup() applies migration 2. Running setup() before rolling out 0.6.0, or granting SELECT on the migrations table, avoids that. The first store call inside a transaction the caller opened gets the permission error once. Only the SELECT grant avoids it.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the vectors table exists with other dims, or its index uses another distance. A different partition size, or an index while flat is set, logs a WARNING instead.

TimeoutError

If another process is still applying migration 2 after SCHEMA_CHANGE_SETTLE_SECONDS. Run setup() again.

Async LangGraph store that keeps long-term memory in CockroachDB.

The async twin of CockroachDBStore: same tables, same SQL, same behavior. For production, pass a psycopg_pool.AsyncConnectionPool or use from_conn_string with pool_config: a pool replaces broken connections, while a single connection cannot recover from a dropped one.

aget, aput, asearch and the other awaited calls, and the sync wrappers, go through AsyncBatchedBaseStore's queue, which runs one abatch at a time. So a pool does not run those calls in parallel, and a large pool does not speed them up. What the queue gives instead is coalescing: ops queued in the same tick run as one batch, with one round trip per read group and one transaction for the writes. Only direct abatch calls, or sync batch calls from other threads, run concurrently on a pool.

The constructor must run inside a running event loop, because AsyncBatchedBaseStore starts a task on it there. Awaited calls made in the same tick (aget, aput, asearch and the others) are coalesced into one abatch. The sync methods (get, put and the others) are meant for other threads while that loop runs. They run the async methods on it, so get, put, search, delete and list_namespaces join the same queue, while batch runs abatch directly. From the loop itself they raise asyncio.InvalidStateError. When the loop is closed or not running, or the call comes from a forked child of the process that created the store, they raise RuntimeError instead of waiting forever, as AsyncCockroachDBSaver's sync methods do.

A batch runs its reads first, then all its puts and deletes in one transaction. Its gets, its searches and its listings take one round trip each. On a store with a vector index, semantic searches under a namespace add one before the searches, to find their namespaces, and one after them when a search must run again exactly. A flat store adds neither. The long-term memory guide explains why.

With history, a batch that overwrites or deletes a memory first copies the version it ends into a history table, in its transaction. adelete then keeps the memory in history; apurge removes a memory with its history, and ahistory lists the old versions.

afind_conflicts, aresolve, areconcile, aconfirm, arecord, aput_if and adelete_if are CockroachDBStore's methods of the same names without the prefix, as coroutines. They run on the caller's event loop, not through the queue, so on a pool they run concurrently. A reconcile policy and a confirm TTL function are plain functions that run on the event loop inside the transaction.

Example 
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBStore

async with AsyncCockroachDBStore.from_conn_string(
    "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"
) as store:
    await store.setup()
    await store.aput(("users", "123"), "prefs", {"theme": "dark"})
    item = await store.aget(("users", "123"), "prefs")

docs.title: aconfirm(namespace, key, *, ttl=NOT_PROVIDED) async
docs.text:
Mark a live memory as confirmed, renewing its expiry and counting confirmations.

The async form of CockroachDBStore.confirm. This counts the confirmation and renews the expiry. That way expiry can follow how often a fact is confirmed, not how often it is read. Confirming does not change the version or updated_at, so it never invalidates a pending afind_conflicts. Confirmations belong to the memory's value: a write that changes it starts them again from none. Each call picks a confirmation id of its own, so a retry after a lost commit counts nothing again, unless another confirmation of the same memory lands in between, in which case the retry counts again. The memory's write id stays as it is.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default namespace tuple[str, ...]

The memory's namespace.

required key str

The memory's key.

required ttl float | None | NotProvided | Callable[[MemoryRecord], float | None]

How long the memory stays after confirmation. NOT_PROVIDED renews from the row's own TTL. None removes the expiry. A number is minutes. A callable takes the MemoryRecord read in the same transaction and returns a number of minutes or None. It is a plain function that runs on the event loop: keep it fast and deterministic, since it runs again on each retry, and it must not call the store. An async function is refused before any I/O.

NOT_PROVIDED

docs.title: adelete_if(namespace, key, *, expected) async
docs.text:
Delete a memory only if it is still the one the caller read, in one transaction.

The async form of CockroachDBStore.delete_if, which describes the retries in full. adelete_if deletes only if the live memory under key still has the version and updated_at of expected, as aput_if checks them. On a match it deletes as adelete does: on a store with history the memory is kept in history as deleted, and its vectors go. With expected=None it applies only while no live memory has the key, so it deletes nothing live.

applied=True means the memory matched expected and this call deleted it, or, after an earlier attempt of the call that may have committed, that the memory is gone and was this call's to delete. On a mismatch it deletes nothing and returns applied=False with current, the live memory as the same transaction read it, or None if there is none. A conflict is returned, not raised.

docs.title: adelete_namespace(namespace_prefix) async
docs.text:
Delete every item in a namespace and its descendants.

("user", "a") deletes ("user", "a") and ("user", "a", "b"), not ("user", "ab"). One statement deletes the items, their vectors and their history. A store without history deletes history too when the history table exists, as when the store kept history before, so nothing of the namespace is left. Its role then needs SELECT and DELETE on that table: without them the whole call fails with a permission error and deletes nothing, rather than forget only part of the namespace.

docs.title: adisable_ttl() async
docs.text:
Turn off CockroachDB row-level TTL on the store's tables.

Expired items are still left out of reads while omit_expired is on. Safe to run from several processes at once. On CockroachDB v25.4 a TTL change fails while another schema change runs on the same table; that error is retried with the budget that schema_change_policy gives it, up to ten minutes by default, even if the policy's retry_on would refuse it. max_attempts=1 turns this off.

docs.title: afind_conflicts(namespace, key, value, *, slot=None, threshold=None, limit=10, filter=None, index=None, ttl=NOT_PROVIDED, provenance=None, valid_at=None) async
docs.text:
Find the memories a new one may conflict with, without writing anything.

The async form of CockroachDBStore.find_conflicts, which describes the candidates in full. They are live memories in namespace itself, for one of three reasons, strongest first: the memory under key; with slot, the memories whose value holds the same value in that field; and on a store with an index, the memories whose vectors score at or above threshold against the new memory's, with the store's score function. Candidates come strongest reason first, then best score, then key. Expired memories are never candidates, and no read pushes back an expiry.

The index fields of value are embedded once, with aembed_documents, and the embedding is kept for aresolve. Then two round trips read the candidates, or three when the C-SPANN index's window may have left matches out.

docs.title: ahistory(namespace, key=None, *, limit=20, offset=0) async
docs.text:
The old versions of a memory, or of every memory in a namespace, newest first.

A store with history keeps every version that a write ends: one a put overwrites (reason "overwritten"), one a delete ends ("deleted"), and one that reconcile or resolve supersedes ("superseded", with superseded_by naming the memory that replaced it). A new memory that reconcile or resolve records as already superseded by a newer fact is kept there too, as "superseded". The live value is not one of them; aget() returns it.

Without a key, it lists the old versions of every memory in exactly namespace, not its descendants, as aget() reads a namespace. That is how to find the old versions of memories that areconcile saved under keys the store generated. Each version carries its own key and superseded_by, so versions can be grouped by a field of their value, or followed to the memory that replaced them. Each call reads the namespace's whole history to sort it, which suits per-user namespaces. For a very large history, page with limit and offset.

docs.title: aput_if(namespace, key, value, *, expected, index=None, ttl=NOT_PROVIDED, provenance=None, valid_at=None) async
docs.text:
Write a memory only if it is still the one the caller read, in one transaction.

The async form of CockroachDBStore.put_if. Two tasks that read the same memory with arecord() and both write it back with aput would lose one update without a word. aput_if writes only if the live memory under key still has the version and updated_at of expected: a put moves the version, and a 0.5.x store, which does not, still moves updated_at. With expected=None it writes only if no live memory has the key, so a memory is created once. An expired memory counts as absent.

On a match it writes as aput does, in the transaction that checked, keeping the version it replaces in history on a store with history. On a mismatch it writes nothing and returns applied=False with current, the live memory as the same transaction read it, or None. A conflict is an expected outcome here, so it is returned, not raised. If an attempt commits and its result is lost, the retry finds the write id on the row and returns applied=True with already_applied. If another writer replaced the memory before the retry, the retry reports a conflict with that writer's memory.

docs.title: areconcile(namespace, key, value, *, policy, slot=None, threshold=None, limit=10, filter=None, index=None, ttl=NOT_PROVIDED, provenance=None, valid_at=None) async
docs.text:
Write a memory and settle the memories it may conflict with, in one transaction.

The async form of CockroachDBStore.reconcile, which describes the decisions and the result in full. The candidates are the ones afind_conflicts finds. They are read in the transaction, policy decides what to do with the new memory and with each candidate, and the decision is applied before the transaction commits. Serializable isolation covers all of it: if another writer changes what the policy saw, one of the two transactions retries, and its policy sees the other's write. Two agents that reconcile contradicting memories for one user cannot both win.

policy is a plain function, not an async one, which is refused before any I/O. It runs on the event loop, inside the transaction, and runs again on every retry, so it must be fast and deterministic: the loop runs nothing else while it runs. An LLM judge, or a person, belongs in afind_conflicts and aresolve, which hold no transaction while the decision is made. A policy must not call the store either: the store holds its connection while the policy runs, so such a call raises RuntimeError at once. A policy that raises rolls the transaction back, and its exception propagates unchanged, without a retry. So does the ValueError for an invalid decision.

The index fields of value are embedded once, with aembed_documents, before the first attempt. If an attempt commits and its result is lost, as when the connection drops while the COMMIT's answer travels, the retry finds the rows that carry its write id and writes nothing. It returns the result rebuilt from those rows, with already_applied set, listing only what the rows prove: kept is empty, and on a store without history so are superseded and deleted.

Narrows the slot and similar candidates by value, as in search.

Which fields of value to embed, as in put.

Minutes the new memory lives once written, or None for no expiry. Defaults to the store's default TTL.

Where the new memory comes from, as a JSON object. It is stored in its own column and kept in history.

docs.title: aresolve(conflicts, decision) async
docs.text:
Apply a decision about what afind_conflicts found, in one transaction.

The async form of CockroachDBStore.resolve, which describes the checks and the retries in full. This is the second step of the two-step flow: afind_conflicts reads the candidates, an LLM or a person decides while no transaction is open, and aresolve applies the decision as areconcile applies a policy's. It writes the new memory that afind_conflicts planned, with its provenance, valid time and write id, and the vectors it embedded then, so nothing is embedded again. For the same reason it refuses a proposal edited after afind_conflicts.

In the same transaction, before it writes, aresolve checks that the memory under the new memory's key, and every candidate the decision supersedes, deletes or confirms, or names as superseding the new memory, still has the version and updated_at that afind_conflicts read. If one changed, it raises ConflictsChanged with those keys, writes nothing and does not retry: find the conflicts again and decide again. Candidates the decision keeps are not checked, and a confirmation in between never counts.

If a resolve of the same Conflicts already committed, aresolve writes nothing and returns that write's result, rebuilt from its rows, with already_applied set. Once an attempt of the call may have committed (it sent its COMMIT and failed with an error other than a serialization failure or a deadlock), a memory the decision supersedes or deletes counts as unchanged when it is gone, for the rest of the call. A Conflicts and a Decision can wait in a LangGraph checkpoint while a person decides: aresolve takes them as the checkpoint gives them back.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default conflicts Conflicts

What afind_conflicts returned, on a store with the same table and index, sync or async.

required decision Decision

What to do with the new memory and each candidate.

required

After a schema read: if setup() has not added the columns this method needs or, on a store with history, created the history table.

docs.title: setup() async
docs.text:
Create the store's tables and run its migrations.

MUST be called the first time the store is used. Safe to run from several processes at once: every migration is idempotent and versions are recorded with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. A setup() that finds another process still applying migration 2 waits for it, for up to SCHEMA_CHANGE_SETTLE_SECONDS, before it records the migration, so no store writes the new columns before they exist. When no job applies the migration, as after a peer's migration failed, it applies the migration itself. With an index, it creates the vectors table and its C-SPANN index (unless flat) on every call, then checks an existing index against the configuration. With history, it creates the history table, and with ttl_days turns on CockroachDB row-level TTL there. With a TTL configuration, it then turns on CockroachDB row-level TTL on expires_at.

It reads a table's TTL settings first and changes them only when they differ from the configuration. On CockroachDB v25.4 a TTL change fails while another schema change runs on the same table, such as a vector index that another setup() builds. That error is retried with the budget that schema_change_policy gives it, up to ten minutes by default for each table, even if the policy's retry_on would refuse it; max_attempts=1 turns this off.

An application role that did not run setup() needs SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the store's items and vectors tables, and on the history table when history is on. With history off, it still needs SELECT and DELETE on a history table that exists, left from when history was on, for delete_namespace. Without SELECT on the migrations table, or without a migrations table, as when the tables were created without setup(), the store finds migration 2 through the items table's columns instead. On a multi-node cluster, one write can then fail in the seconds after setup() applies migration 2. Running setup() before rolling out 0.6.0, or granting SELECT on the migrations table, avoids that. The first store call inside a transaction the caller opened gets the permission error once. Only the SELECT grant avoids it.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the vectors table exists with other dims, or its index uses another distance. A different partition size, or an index while flat is set, logs a WARNING instead.

TimeoutError

If another process is still applying migration 2 after SCHEMA_CHANGE_SETTLE_SECONDS. Run setup() again.

docs.title: ReconcileResult

docs.title: langchain_cockroachdb.store.reconcile.ReconcileResult dataclass
docs.text:
What a reconcile or resolve did.

An attempt can commit and still lose its result on the way back, as when the connection drops while the COMMIT's answer travels. The retry then finds the rows that carry its write id, writes nothing, and returns a result rebuilt from those rows, with already_applied set. A rebuilt result lists only what the rows prove: kept is empty, and superseded and deleted come from the history rows the write created, so a store without history, which keeps no trace of what it removed, reports them empty too. A confirmation of the new memory before the retry leaves the write's proof on it. If another writer replaced the new memory before the retry, the history row of the version the write overwrote, or of a memory it superseded, still proves the write: the result says "written", but its version is None. A rebuilt result lists keys in key order; a normal one in the order of the candidates.

Attributes:

Name Type Description key str

The new memory's key, whether it was written or not.

new Literal['written', 'skipped', 'superseded']

What happened to the new memory: "written", "skipped", or "superseded" when it went straight into history because a newer fact supersedes it. A store without history skips such a memory, and the result says "skipped".

version int | None

The version written, or None when nothing was written. A rebuilt result also has None for a written memory that another writer replaced before the retry.

superseded tuple[str, ...]

Keys of the candidates the new memory superseded.

deleted tuple[str, ...]

Keys of the candidates deleted.

confirmed tuple[str, ...]

Keys of the candidates confirmed.

kept tuple[str, ...]

Keys of the candidates kept. The memory under the new key is not kept when the new memory overwrote it.

already_applied bool

Whether an earlier attempt had already committed, so the result was rebuilt from the stored rows.

docs.title: RECONCILE_SERDE_TYPES
docs.text: The classes a checkpoint serializer must allow, so reconcile values can wait in graph state.

Every class a reconcile value can hold, as (module, class name) pairs.

A strict checkpoint serializer rebuilds only the classes it is given and gives any other back raw, as LangGraph's does with LANGGRAPH_STRICT_MSGPACK=true. To keep a Conflicts, a Decision, a ReconcileResult, a ConditionalWrite, a MemoryRecord or a MemoryVersion in graph state, give the checkpointer a serializer that allows these: JsonPlusSerializer(allowed_msgpack_modules=RECONCILE_SERDE_TYPES), with your own state's types added if they are not built in. The pairs are the form that allowed_msgpack_modules takes, from langgraph-checkpoint 4.0.1. Before 4.0.1, JsonPlusSerializer has no allowed_msgpack_modules argument, and passing it raises TypeError; those releases rebuild every class.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text: A policy is a function of the Proposal and the sequence of candidates that returns a Decision, typed as Policy (Callable[[Proposal, Sequence[Candidate]], Decision]). It runs inside the reconcile's transaction, and again on every retry, so it must be a plain function, fast and deterministic, and must not call the store. These are the built-in ones, and validate_decision, which checks a decision as reconcile and resolve do.

docs.title: langchain_cockroachdb.store.reconcile.supersede_same_slot()
docs.text:
Return a policy that supersedes older facts in the same slot.

  1. If the memory under the proposal's key (the target) has a later valid_at, skip the proposal, whatever reason the target has.
  2. Otherwise, if no candidate is in the same slot (reason "slot"), write the proposal and keep every candidate.
  3. If a slot candidate has a later valid_at, record the proposal as superseded by the latest such candidate.
  4. Otherwise, supersede all slot candidates.

Returns:

Type Description Policy

Policy that supersedes same-slot candidates.

docs.title: langchain_cockroachdb.store.reconcile.skip_duplicates(threshold=0.97)
docs.text:
Return a policy that skips a memory that repeats one already stored.

A new memory, one with no live memory under its key, is skipped when a candidate has an equal value or scores at or above threshold, and the highest-scoring such candidate is confirmed (an equal value counts as score 1.0). When the proposal has a slot, only candidates in the same slot count: a repeat outside the slot states another fact, and skipping the new memory for it would leave an older memory in the slot live, which may contradict the new one. A memory whose key holds a live memory is skipped only when it saves that memory's value again, which confirms it. Any other value there is an update, which this policy never skips, whatever repeats it under another key: skipping it would leave the key with its old value, which may contradict the new one. Then it returns the decision that writes the new memory and keeps every candidate, so first_of moves on to the next policy.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default threshold float

Similarity threshold (default 0.97).

0.97

Returns:

Type Description Policy

Policy that skips duplicates.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If threshold is not a finite number.

docs.title: langchain_cockroachdb.store.reconcile.supersede_similar(threshold=0.9)
docs.text:

Works like supersede_same_slot, but matches the slot candidates and the candidates scoring at or above threshold. As there, a target with a later valid_at skips the proposal whatever it scores, and so does a target without a score, as on a store without an index.

docs.title: langchain_cockroachdb.async_vectorstore.AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore
docs.text:
Bases: VectorStore

Async vector store using CockroachDB native VECTOR type and C-SPANN indexes.

Every database call retries transient CockroachDB errors under retry_policy, which defaults to the engine's policy. Every write is an idempotent UPSERT or DELETE, so retrying after an ambiguous result is safe.

A search with a metadata filter uses the C-SPANN index when the table has one that can serve it: it ranks the nearest rows from the index, filters them, and runs the exact search when they may have left matches out. See "Filtered search" in the vector indexes guide.

docs.title: CockroachDBEngine
docs.text:
Purpose: Connection and transaction management

Key Features: - AsyncEngine from SQLAlchemy - Connection pooling - Retry configuration - Table initialization

Pattern: 

engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(url)
# Engine manages connection lifecycle
await engine.aclose()

docs.title: AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore
docs.text:
Purpose: Primary vector store implementation

Key Features: - Async-first design - Batch operations - Metadata filtering - Index management

Pattern: 

vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine=engine,
    embeddings=embeddings,
    collection_name="docs",
)
await vectorstore.aadd_texts(texts)

docs.title: CockroachDBVectorStore
docs.text:
Purpose: Synchronous wrapper for async operations

Implementation: - Runs async methods on one background event loop - Same API as async version (without a prefix) - Safe from any number of threads and from inside a running event loop

Pattern: 

vectorstore = CockroachDBVectorStore(...)  # Sync
vectorstore.add_texts(texts)  # No await

docs.title: Async-First Architecture
docs.text:
All I/O operations are async by default:

# Core operations
async def aadd_texts(texts: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    async with self.engine.engine.connect() as conn:
        # Async database operations
        ...

Benefits: - High concurrency - Better resource utilization - Natural fit for modern Python

docs.title: Retry Decorators
docs.text:
Each idempotent statement is wrapped by RetryPolicy.arun. The callable passed to arun checks out a fresh connection per attempt:

async def aadd_texts(texts: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    async def attempt():
        async with self.engine._connect() as conn:
            return await conn.execute(insert_statement, params)

    await self.retry_policy.arun(attempt, label="insert into documents")

Benefits: - Transparent retry logic - Configurable per component - Handles transient CockroachDB errors automatically - Fresh connection per retry

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Engine is injected into vector store:

vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine=engine,  # Injected dependency
    embeddings=embeddings,
    collection_name="docs",
)

Benefits: - Testable (can mock engine) - Flexible configuration - Connection reuse

docs.title: Filter Translation
docs.text:
Metadata filters are translated to SQL:

filter = {"category": "tech", "year": {"$gte": 2023}}

# Becomes:
WHERE metadata->>'category' = 'tech'
  AND CAST(metadata->>'year' AS INTEGER) >= 2023

docs.title: Distance Operators
docs.text:
Different distance strategies use different operators:

Strategy Operator SQL COSINE <=> ORDER BY embedding <=> :query EUCLIDEAN <-> ORDER BY embedding <-> :query INNER_PRODUCT <#> ORDER BY embedding <#> :query

docs.title: Retryable Errors
docs.text:
SQLSTATE Meaning Why a retry is safe 40001 Serialization failure ("restart transaction") The transaction did not commit 40003 Result is ambiguous Every write the library issues is idempotent 08xxx Connection exceptions, including CockroachDB sqlproxy's 08C00 Idempotent writes, and the pool replaces the connection 57P01 Node draining or shutting down Idempotent writes 58C00 Range unavailable (CockroachDB) Usually clears once leases move 58C01 Connection failure between CockroachDB nodes Usually clears once leases move 53300 Too many connections Connection slots free up

Errors without a SQLSTATE and CockroachDB's uncategorized codes (XXUUU, XX000) are matched against known connection-loss phrases.

See Retries and Resilience for full details.

docs.title: Fault Injection
docs.text:
The tests/integration/faults.py module provides three mechanisms for injecting real CockroachDB faults:

  1. FaultInjector - for SQLAlchemy async engine (vector store, chat history). Swaps faulted statements for crdb_internal.force_error so the server raises the error during normal execution and SQLAlchemy wraps it.

  2. PsycopgFaults - for raw psycopg connections (checkpointers). Uses cursor_factory to check for a pending fault before every cursor execute.

  3. kill_sessions and hold_row_lock - helper functions to cancel sessions (simulating node restarts or load balancer resets) and hold row locks (simulating stuck ranges).

These let tests verify that the retry policy handles real CockroachDB errors exactly as they would appear in production.

docs.title: Application-process Recovery
docs.text:
test_graph_process_recovery.py exercises real LangGraph workflows with both checkpointers. Each worker runs three independent conversations through one pool capped at two connections. The parent kills that worker and starts a fresh process, so the resumed application cannot reuse its graph, event loop, connection pool, or Python state.

The suite covers two crash boundaries:

  • A graph has saved a human-approval interrupt. The fresh application resumes it with Command(resume=...) and the same thread ID.
  • One parallel node has committed pending writes while another is blocked. The fresh application resumes with None, reuses the successful node's output, and reruns the unfinished node.

Pipe notifications wait for committed pending writes and blocked nodes before the parent kills the process. No fixed sleeps choose the crash point. The parent also reads the database between processes to check saved state and pending writes, then verifies distinct results for every thread after resume. For approvals, it compares the saved interrupt's payload and identity with the interrupt returned by the graph. Completed states must match each thread's expected values and have no pending writes. Each test deletes only its own randomly generated thread IDs.

The workers use durability="sync" so parent checkpoints commit before the next graph step starts. LangGraph's "async" durability mode can lose a checkpoint on process failure while it is being saved. See LangGraph's durability modes. These are separate choices from using sync or async Python APIs; both APIs are tested with synchronous checkpoint durability. On Python 3.10, LangGraph's interrupt() works only with the sync API, because an async graph's tasks carry no run-config context before Python 3.11, so the async approval case is skipped there.

A file log outside the checkpointer records node effects across the crash. The assertions verify that a successful node with saved pending writes does not repeat, while code before an interrupt or unfinished node boundary runs again. This does not guarantee exactly-once external tool execution. A crash after an external effect and before its pending write commits can repeat the effect; applications need idempotency keys or reconciliation for that case.

Run against a disposable CockroachDB instance with the normal fixture, or use an existing test instance:

USE_TESTCONTAINER=false \
COCKROACHDB_URL='postgresql://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable' \
.venv/bin/pytest tests/integration/test_graph_process_recovery.py -v

The tests need the development langgraph dependency and skip when it is not installed, including CI's minimum runtime dependency job. No model API keys are needed. The database stays online throughout: database restarts, physical cluster replication, failover, and recovery-time measurements require separate infrastructure and are not covered here.

docs.title: Graph Recovery After Connection Loss
docs.text:
test_graph_connection_recovery.py runs a deterministic two-node LangGraph workflow with sync and async pooled checkpointers. A completed preparation node arms the test cursor to close its own checked-out connection immediately before the next checkpoint INSERT. Psycopg raises the closed-connection error during normal execution. This fault uses client-side connection closure: it does not simulate a network partition, terminate server sessions, or restart a database. It needs no unsafe CockroachDB internals or server administration privileges.

Each Python API has two cases:

  • One closed connection is replaced by the pool, and the saver retries the checkpoint without failing the graph invocation.
  • Three consecutive closed connections exhaust a policy of three total attempts. The graph invocation raises the driver error. The test verifies the exact number of closed connections, two retry warnings, and one exhaustion warning. It then reads the durable input checkpoint and the preparation node's pending writes before explicitly resuming the graph with invoke(None, config) or ainvoke(None, config).

Both cases verify the final persisted state and exactly one execution of each node. The pool is capped at one connection to make replacement observable; concurrent pool usage is covered separately by the process-recovery tests. Each test uses durability="sync", an independent random thread ID, and only deletes its own thread's data. No model calls or fixed sleeps select the failure boundary.

The no-replay assertion applies to a node whose pending writes already committed. If an external tool succeeds before its pending writes commit, an application failure can still cause that tool to run again. Applications need idempotency keys or reconciliation for those effects. These tests also do not establish recovery guarantees for ambiguous commits, real network outages, or database failover.

Run the four cases on a disposable CockroachDB instance:

USE_TESTCONTAINER=false \
COCKROACHDB_URL='postgresql://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable' \
.venv/bin/pytest tests/integration/test_graph_connection_recovery.py -v

The tests require the development langgraph dependency and skip when it is absent. They use the normal integration fixtures and work without paid model credentials.

docs.title: Provisioned Virtual Clusters
docs.text:
tests/integration/test_virtual_cluster_deployment.py is an opt-in suite for two disposable application virtual clusters. It accepts their complete SQL URLs, including the supplied TLS and routing parameters. It does not start a testcontainer, provision resources, change users, or alter network access. For a managed Continuum host, use two of the host's virtual clusters, each with its own connection string. For self-hosted testing, use one virtualized cluster and compare the main and system virtual clusters (primary on -ccluster%3Dmain, peer on -ccluster%3Dsystem): two physical clusters both on -ccluster%3Dmain would not catch a dropped options value, since each connection would still reach its own cluster's default virtual cluster. Different URL strings alone do not establish that the targets are distinct virtual clusters; verify their deployment metadata first.

The tests write different values under identical table names, document IDs, session IDs, and checkpoint IDs on both targets. They check vector insert, lookup, search and deletion, chat persistence and clearing, and sync/async checkpoint and pending-write round trips. Removing data from the first target must leave the peer's data intact. Randomly named tables and threads are cleaned up after the run; existing application data is not targeted. Checkpointer setup leaves its normal tables and migrations in place.

Set COCKROACHDB_VIRTUAL_CLUSTER_URL and COCKROACHDB_VIRTUAL_CLUSTER_PEER_URL to two separate test virtual clusters. For a managed Continuum host, obtain each virtual cluster's connection string from its own Connect dialog or ccloud. A host cluster's console URL is not a SQL endpoint. For self-hosted virtualization, keep the URL's percent-encoded -ccluster option. The SQL users need permission to create and drop the test tables and set up checkpoint tables in the chosen databases.

These checks establish data routing and deletion isolation for the supplied targets. They do not test authorization, failover, or the supported number of virtual clusters on a host. Driver failures report the error class and SQLSTATE without a connection traceback because driver arguments may contain passwords.

All four cases have been run against two virtual clusters on a Cockroach Continuum host cluster (CockroachDB v26.3.1) and passed, confirming that vector data, chat history, and sync and async checkpoints stay isolated to their own virtual cluster.

Keep credentials in a local, ignored .env.local file, then run:

uv run --no-sync --env-file .env.local pytest tests/integration/test_virtual_cluster_deployment.py -v

Without both variables the four tests skip, including in regular CI. Never commit URLs containing passwords. No model API keys are used. Run this suite against designated test targets because it creates and removes its own data.

import pytest
from langchain_core.embeddings import DeterministicFakeEmbedding
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore, CockroachDBEngine


class TestVectorStore:
    @pytest.mark.asyncio
    async def test_add_and_search(self, connection_string: str):
        """Test adding documents and searching."""
        # Setup
        engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(connection_string)
        await engine.ainit_vectorstore_table(
            table_name="test_docs",
            vector_dimension=384,
            drop_if_exists=True,
        )

        embeddings = DeterministicFakeEmbedding(size=384)
        vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
            engine=engine,
            embeddings=embeddings,
            collection_name="test_docs",
        )

        # Test
        texts = ["doc1", "doc2", "doc3"]
        ids = await vectorstore.aadd_texts(texts)

        assert len(ids) == 3

        results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search("doc1", k=2)

        assert len(results) == 2
        assert results[0].page_content in texts

        # Cleanup
        await engine.aclose()

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Complete example from zero to searching in 5 minutes.

File: examples/quickstart.py

import asyncio
import os
from langchain_core.embeddings import DeterministicFakeEmbedding
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore, CockroachDBEngine

async def main():
    # 1. Initialize engine
    engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(
        os.getenv("COCKROACHDB_URL", 
                  "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable")
    )

    # 2. Create table
    await engine.ainit_vectorstore_table(
        table_name="quickstart",
        vector_dimension=384,
        drop_if_exists=True,
    )

    # 3. Initialize vector store
    embeddings = DeterministicFakeEmbedding(size=384)
    vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
        engine=engine,
        embeddings=embeddings,
        collection_name="quickstart",
    )

    # 4. Add documents
    texts = [
        "CockroachDB is a distributed SQL database",
        "LangChain makes building LLM apps easy",
        "Vector search enables semantic similarity",
    ]
    ids = await vectorstore.aadd_texts(texts)
    print(f"✅ Added {len(ids)} documents")

    # 5. Search
    results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(
        "Tell me about databases",
        k=2
    )

    print("\n🔍 Search Results:")
    for i, doc in enumerate(results, 1):
        print(f"{i}. {doc.page_content}")

    # 6. Cleanup
    await engine.aclose()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Output: 

✅ Added 3 documents

🔍 Search Results:
1. CockroachDB is a distributed SQL database
2. Vector search enables semantic similarity

import os
from langchain_core.embeddings import DeterministicFakeEmbedding
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBVectorStore, CockroachDBEngine

def main():
    # Initialize (no async/await needed)
    engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(
        os.getenv("COCKROACHDB_URL")
    )

    engine.init_vectorstore_table(
        table_name="sync_demo",
        vector_dimension=384,
        drop_if_exists=True,
    )

    embeddings = DeterministicFakeEmbedding(size=384)
    vectorstore = CockroachDBVectorStore(
        engine=engine,
        embeddings=embeddings,
        collection_name="sync_demo",
    )

    # Add documents (sync)
    texts = ["Document 1", "Document 2", "Document 3"]
    ids = vectorstore.add_texts(texts)
    print(f"Added {len(ids)} documents")

    # Search (sync)
    results = vectorstore.similarity_search("document", k=2)
    for doc in results:
        print(f"- {doc.page_content}")

    # Cleanup
    engine.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Chat History
docs.text:
Persistent conversation storage.

File: examples/chat_history.py

import os
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBChatMessageHistory
from langchain.chains import ConversationChain
from langchain.memory import ConversationBufferMemory
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

def main():
    # Initialize chat history
    history = CockroachDBChatMessageHistory(
        session_id="user-123",
        connection_string=os.getenv("COCKROACHDB_URL"),
    )

    # Create memory
    memory = ConversationBufferMemory(
        chat_memory=history,
        return_messages=True,
    )

    # Create chatbot
    chatbot = ConversationChain(
        llm=ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4"),
        memory=memory,
        verbose=True,
    )

    # First interaction
    response1 = chatbot.predict(input="My name is Alice")
    print(f"Bot: {response1}")

    # Later interaction (history is remembered)
    response2 = chatbot.predict(input="What's my name?")
    print(f"Bot: {response2}")

    # View history
    messages = history.messages
    print(f"\n📝 Chat history: {len(messages)} messages")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Chatbot with Memory
docs.text:
Complete example of a LangGraph chatbot with persistent memory:

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START, END
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver

llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")


def chatbot(state: MessagesState):
    return {"messages": [llm.invoke(state["messages"])]}


graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)
graph.add_node("chatbot", chatbot)
graph.add_edge(START, "chatbot")
graph.add_edge("chatbot", END)

DB_URI = "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"

with CockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as checkpointer:
    checkpointer.setup()
    app = graph.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "session-1"}}

    # Multi-turn conversation with memory
    app.invoke({"messages": [("user", "My name is Alice")]}, config)
    result = app.invoke({"messages": [("user", "What is my name?")]}, config)
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)  # Should remember "Alice"

docs.title: Human-in-the-Loop
docs.text:
Interrupt and resume workflow execution:

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START, END
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver


def propose(state: MessagesState):
    return {"messages": [("assistant", "Proposed action: send email")]}


def execute(state: MessagesState):
    return {"messages": [("assistant", "Email sent successfully")]}


graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)
graph.add_node("propose", propose)
graph.add_node("execute", execute)
graph.add_edge(START, "propose")
graph.add_edge("propose", "execute")
graph.add_edge("execute", END)

DB_URI = "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"

with CockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as checkpointer:
    checkpointer.setup()
    app = graph.compile(
        checkpointer=checkpointer,
        interrupt_before=["execute"],
    )

    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "approval-1"}}

    # Step 1: Runs "propose", pauses before "execute"
    result = app.invoke({"messages": [("user", "Send the report")]}, config)
    print("Waiting for approval...")

    # Step 2: Human approves, resume execution
    result = app.invoke(None, config)
    print(result["messages"][-1])

docs.title: Row-Level TTL (Automatic Expiry)
docs.text:
Enable automatic cleanup of old checkpoint data using CockroachDB's row-level TTL:

from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver

DB_URI = "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"

with CockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as saver:
    saver.setup()

    # Expire checkpoints older than 7 days, clean up hourly
    saver.enable_ttl(ttl_interval="7 days", cron="@hourly")

    # Use the checkpointer normally
    graph = workflow.compile(checkpointer=saver)
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-123"}}
    result = graph.invoke({"messages": [("user", "Hello!")]}, config)

    # To disable TTL later:
    # saver.disable_ttl()

Async variant:

from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBSaver

async with AsyncCockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as saver:
    await saver.setup()
    await saver.aenable_ttl(ttl_interval="30 days", cron="@daily")

docs.title: Index Optimization
docs.text:
Performance optimization with C-SPANN indexes.

File: examples/vector_indexes.py

docs.title: Creating Indexes
docs.text:
from langchain_cockroachdb import CSPANNIndex, DistanceStrategy

# Basic index
index = CSPANNIndex()
await vectorstore.aapply_vector_index(index)

# With distance strategy
index = CSPANNIndex(distance_strategy=DistanceStrategy.COSINE)
await vectorstore.aapply_vector_index(index)

# With partition tuning
index = CSPANNIndex(
    min_partition_size=10,
    max_partition_size=100,
)
await vectorstore.aapply_vector_index(index)

docs.title: Performance Comparison
docs.text:
import time

# Without index
start = time.time()
results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search("query", k=10)
no_index_time = time.time() - start

# Create index
index = CSPANNIndex()
await vectorstore.aapply_vector_index(index)

# With index
start = time.time()
results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search("query", k=10)
with_index_time = time.time() - start

print(f"Without index: {no_index_time*1000:.1f}ms")
print(f"With index: {with_index_time*1000:.1f}ms")
print(f"Speedup: {no_index_time/with_index_time:.1f}x")

docs.title: Query-Time Tuning
docs.text:
from langchain_cockroachdb import CSPANNQueryOptions

# The default beam size is 32. A larger beam is more accurate and slower
results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(
    "query", k=10, query_options=CSPANNQueryOptions(beam_size=64)
)

# A smaller beam is faster and less accurate
results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(
    "query", k=10, query_options=CSPANNQueryOptions(beam_size=16)
)

The store sets the beam size with SET LOCAL in the search's own transaction. A SET on a connection you open yourself does not reach the store's searches, which run on connections from the pool.

docs.title: Long-Term Memory Example
docs.text: examples/long_term_memory.py gives a LangGraph agent long-term memory in CockroachDB. The agent saves a memory in one conversation thread and finds it again, by semantic search, in another thread.

docs.title: Running the Example
docs.text:
# Install the package, and langchain for create_agent (it also installs langgraph)
pip install langchain-cockroachdb langchain

# Start CockroachDB
docker-compose up -d

# Run the long-term memory example
python examples/long_term_memory.py

It needs no API key. The chat model is scripted, and the embeddings come from DeterministicFakeEmbedding, which gives each text a fixed random vector. That does not rank by meaning, so the example keeps one memory per user at a time. A real embedding model ranks by meaning with the same code.

The store uses its own tables (memory_example, memory_example_vectors and memory_example_migrations) and drops them at the end, even after a failure. The checkpointer uses the default checkpoint tables, and the example deletes its threads from them.

docs.title: The Store and the Checkpointer on One Pool
docs.text:
The store gets semantic search (index) and expiry (ttl). The checkpointer keeps each thread's messages, and shares the pool:

INDEX = {"dims": 64, "embed": DeterministicFakeEmbedding(size=64), "fields": ["text"]}
# default_ttl is in minutes: items expire 30 days after they were written or last read
TTL = {"default_ttl": 60 * 24 * 30, "refresh_on_read": True}

with ConnectionPool(
    LIBPQ_URL,
    min_size=1,
    max_size=4,
    kwargs={"autocommit": True, "row_factory": dict_row},
    open=True,
) as pool:
    store = CockroachDBStore(pool, index=INDEX, ttl=TTL, table_name=TABLE)
    store.setup()
    checkpointer = CockroachDBSaver(pool)
    checkpointer.setup()

The application can also write items itself. The profile is never embedded and never expires. Bob's memory shows that searches and deletes stay inside one user's namespace:

store.put(("user", "alice", "profile"), "name", {"name": "Alice"}, index=False, ttl=None)
store.put(("user", "bob", "memories"), "seat", {"text": "I prefer aisle seats."})

docs.title: Tools That Use the Store
docs.text:
Tools reach the store through ToolRuntime, and the user id comes from the run's context. ToolRuntime takes two type arguments, the context and the agent state. Give both: Python 3.10 cannot fill in the default of the second, and a plain ToolRuntime expects no context, so pydantic warns about the Context it gets.

@dataclass
class Context:
    """Who the agent is talking to, passed with each call."""

    user_id: str


def memories(runtime: ToolRuntime[Context, dict]) -> tuple[str, ...]:
    """The namespace of the current user's memories."""
    return ("user", runtime.context.user_id, "memories")


@tool
def save_memory(text: str, runtime: ToolRuntime[Context, dict]) -> str:
    """Save a fact about the user for later conversations."""
    assert runtime.store is not None
    runtime.store.put(memories(runtime), str(uuid.uuid4()), {"text": text})
    return f"Saved to {memories(runtime)}: {text}"


@tool
def recall(query: str, runtime: ToolRuntime[Context, dict]) -> str:
    """Search the user's memories."""
    assert runtime.store is not None
    found = runtime.store.search(memories(runtime), query=query, limit=1)
    return f"From memory: {found[0].value['text']}" if found else "I have no memories of you."

docs.title: Two Threads, One Memory
docs.text:
Each message starts a new thread, so the second thread has none of the first one's messages. The answer comes from the store:

agent = create_agent(
    ScriptedModel(),
    tools=[save_memory, recall],
    context_schema=Context,
    checkpointer=checkpointer,
    store=store,
)
alice = Context(user_id="alice")
for thread, text in [
    ("thread-1", "Remember that I prefer window seats."),
    ("thread-2", "Where do I like to sit on a plane?"),
]:
    result = agent.invoke(
        {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": text}]},
        {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread}},
        context=alice,
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)

docs.title: Namespaces and Deleting a User
docs.text:
store.list_namespaces(prefix=("user", "alice"))
# [('user', 'alice', 'memories'), ('user', 'alice', 'profile')]

store.delete_namespace(("user", "alice"))  # 2, the memory and the profile
store.list_namespaces(prefix=("user",))
# [('user', 'bob', 'memories')]

docs.title: The Async Version
docs.text:
The second half builds AsyncCockroachDBStore with from_conn_string and pool_config, and its tools await the store's aput and asearch:

async with (
    AsyncCockroachDBStore.from_conn_string(
        CONNECTION_STRING,
        pool_config={"min_size": 1, "max_size": 4},
        index=INDEX,
        ttl=TTL,
        table_name=TABLE,
    ) as store,
    AsyncCockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(CONNECTION_STRING) as checkpointer,
):
    await store.setup()
    await checkpointer.setup()
    ...
    removed = await store.adelete_namespace(("user",))  # every user's items

docs.text:

docs.title: Memory Reconciliation Example
docs.text: examples/memory_reconciliation.py keeps an agent's long-term memory true. A newer fact supersedes an older one in the same slot, a repeated fact confirms the memory it repeats, and a fact that arrives late goes straight into history. A judge decides about a conflict in two steps, history keeps every old version with its provenance, confirm renews a memory's expiry, and put_if keeps two writers from losing an update. It ends with the forget path.

docs.title: Running the Example
docs.text:
# Install the package
pip install langchain-cockroachdb

# Start CockroachDB
docker-compose up -d

# Run the memory reconciliation example
python examples/memory_reconciliation.py

It needs no API key. KeywordEmbeddings, defined in the script, stands in for an embedding model. It gives each text one dimension for each keyword the text mentions. So texts that share keywords score high against each other, as a real model scores texts about the same thing. "I prefer aisle seats now." and "Aisle seats, please." score 0.99, and the window and aisle preferences score 0.50. The judge in the two-step flow is a scripted function that stands in for an LLM or a person.

The store uses its own tables (memory_reconciliation, memory_reconciliation_vectors, memory_reconciliation_history and memory_reconciliation_migrations) and drops them at the end, even after a failure. The script gives its memories readable keys. An agent usually passes None as the key, and the store picks a uuid4.

docs.title: The Store
docs.text:
History is on, so every write that ends a version keeps it. Expiry follows confirmations, not reads:

INDEX: CockroachDBIndexConfig = {
    "dims": len(KeywordEmbeddings.WEIGHTS) + 1,
    "embed": KeywordEmbeddings(),
    "fields": ["text"],
}
# Memories expire 30 days after they were written or last confirmed. Reads do
# not push back the expiry: retrieval is not confirmation
TTL: CockroachDBTTLConfig = {"default_ttl": 30 * DAY, "refresh_on_read": False}
# Keep old versions for a year
HISTORY: HistoryConfig = {"ttl_days": 365}

with CockroachDBStore.from_conn_string(
    CONNECTION_STRING, index=INDEX, ttl=TTL, history=HISTORY, table_name=TABLE
) as store:
    store.setup()

Each memory about where Alice sits has "slot": "seat". The policy skips a near duplicate and confirms the memory it repeats. Otherwise it lets a newer fact in the same slot supersede the older ones:

POLICY = first_of(skip_duplicates(), supersede_same_slot())

docs.title: A Newer Fact Supersedes the Older One
docs.text:
Alice said she prefers window seats in January, and the agent passes that as the memory's valid time. Later she prefers aisle seats. The second reconcile finds the first memory in the same slot, and the policy supersedes it, in the transaction that writes the new one:

store.reconcile(
    MEMORIES,
    "seat-window",
    in_seat_slot("I prefer window seats."),
    slot="slot",
    policy=POLICY,
    provenance={"source": "chat", "thread": "thread-1"},
    valid_at=datetime(2026, 1, 15, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
)
store.reconcile(
    MEMORIES,
    "seat-aisle",
    in_seat_slot("I prefer aisle seats now."),
    slot="slot",
    policy=POLICY,
    provenance={"source": "chat", "thread": "thread-2"},
)

Then record reads the aisle preference with its version and provenance.

docs.title: A Near Duplicate Confirms the Memory It Repeats
docs.text:
"Aisle seats, please." scores 0.99 against the aisle preference, so skip_duplicates writes nothing and confirms the memory it repeats. Repeating a fact reinforces it instead of piling up copies:

result = store.reconcile(
    MEMORIES,
    "seat-aisle-again",
    in_seat_slot("Aisle seats, please."),
    slot="slot",
    policy=POLICY,
    provenance={"source": "chat", "thread": "thread-3"},
)
# result.new == "skipped", result.confirmed == ("seat-aisle",)

docs.title: A Late Fact Goes Straight Into History
docs.text:
The agent reads an old conversation from March 2025, where Alice said she prefers window seats. The aisle preference became true later, so supersede_same_slot records the old fact as superseded by it. With history on, the fact goes straight into history and never becomes live:

result = store.reconcile(
    MEMORIES,
    "seat-window-2025",
    in_seat_slot("I prefer window seats."),
    slot="slot",
    policy=POLICY,
    provenance={"source": "chat", "thread": "thread-2025-03"},
    valid_at=datetime(2025, 3, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
)
# result.new == "superseded"

A search of the seat slot still finds only the aisle preference.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
history returns the old versions of a memory, newest first. Each one says when its fact was true, why it ended, what replaced it and where it came from:

for key in ("seat-window", "seat-window-2025"):
    for version in store.history(MEMORIES, key):
        print(key, version.version, version.value["text"])
        print(version.valid_at, version.invalid_at, version.reason, version.superseded_by)
        print(version.provenance)

docs.title: Two Steps With a Judge
docs.text:
A tool that knows nothing of reconciliation saved "Allergic to peanuts." with a plain put. Now Alice says she is no longer allergic. find_conflicts finds the old memory as a similar candidate (score 0.90), and the judge decides to supersede it. No transaction is open while the judge decides, so the script lets another writer change the old memory in between. resolve notices, raises ConflictsChanged and writes nothing. The script finds the conflicts again, asks the judge again, and resolve applies the decision:

def judge(conflicts: Conflicts) -> Decision:
    """Stands in for an LLM or a person deciding about the conflicts.

    A memory that says something is no longer true supersedes the similar
    memories it contradicts. Anything else is written next to them.
    """
    if "no longer" in conflicts.proposal.value["text"].lower():
        similar = [c.key for c in conflicts.candidates if c.reason == "similar"]
        return Decision(actions={key: Action.SUPERSEDE for key in similar})
    return Decision()


store.put(MEMORIES, "allergy", {"text": "Allergic to peanuts."})
new = {"text": "No longer allergic to peanuts."}
conflicts = find(store, "no-peanut-allergy", new)
decision = judge(conflicts)
store.put(MEMORIES, "allergy", {"text": "Allergic to peanuts and cashews."})  # another writer
try:
    store.resolve(conflicts, decision)
except ConflictsChanged as changed:
    print(changed.keys)  # ('allergy',)
conflicts = find(store, "no-peanut-allergy", new)
result = store.resolve(conflicts, judge(conflicts))

find is a helper in the script that calls find_conflicts and prints the candidates. With an LLM in place of judge, the code is the same, as the guide's example shows.

docs.title: Confirmation-Driven Expiry
docs.text:
confirm renews a memory's expiry and counts the confirmation. Its ttl here is a function of the memory, so each confirmation keeps the memory longer:

def renewal(record: MemoryRecord) -> float:
    """Minutes a confirmed memory stays: 30 days, doubled for each earlier confirmation.

    At most a year. ``record`` is the memory as confirm read it, before this
    confirmation counts.
    """
    return min(30 * DAY * 2.0**record.confirmations, 365 * DAY)


store.confirm(MEMORIES, "seat-aisle", ttl=renewal)

The aisle preference was confirmed once already, by the duplicate, so the next two confirmations keep it 60 and then 120 days. Items do not carry their expiry, so the script reads it from the table to show it. Confirming a memory that does not exist returns False.

docs.title: Two Writers
docs.text:
put_if with expected=None creates a memory only if no live memory has the key, so the second attempt to create it is a conflict. Then two writers read the same version with record and both add an airline. The first put_if applies. The second is a conflict, and its result carries the current memory, so the writer merges with it and writes again, expecting it:

def add_airline(
    store: CockroachDBStore, record: MemoryRecord | None, name: str, writer: str
) -> ConditionalWrite:
    """Add an airline to the memory read as ``record``, merging if another writer changed it."""
    while True:
        names = record.item.value["airlines"] if record else []
        result = store.put_if(MEMORIES, "airlines", airlines([*names, name]), expected=record)
        if result.applied:
            print(f"   {writer} adds {name}: applied, version {result.version}")
            return result
        # Another writer got there first: merge with the current memory, and expect it
        record = result.current
        current = "none" if record is None else f"version {record.version}"
        print(f"   {writer} adds {name}: conflict, the current memory is {current}")


store.put_if(MEMORIES, "airlines", airlines(["TAP"]), expected=None)  # applied, version 1
store.put_if(MEMORIES, "airlines", airlines(["TAP"]), expected=None)  # a conflict
first = store.record(MEMORIES, "airlines")
second = store.record(MEMORIES, "airlines")
add_airline(store, first, "Iberia", "writer 1")
add_airline(store, second, "KLM", "writer 2")  # conflict, then merged

Neither update is lost: the memory ends at version 3 with both airlines.

docs.title: Forgetting
docs.text:
With history on, delete keeps the version it ends, and get no longer finds the memory. purge removes the memory with its vectors and its history. It also clears the history of a memory that was superseded:

store.delete(MEMORIES, "airlines")
store.history(MEMORIES, "airlines")  # versions 3 (deleted), 2 and 1 (overwritten)
store.purge(MEMORIES, "airlines")  # True
store.purge(MEMORIES, "seat-window")  # True

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
setup() created the store tables, with history, a vector index and TTL

1. A newer fact in the same slot supersedes the older one
   reconcile seat-window: written, version 1
   reconcile seat-aisle: written, version 1, superseded ['seat-window']
   record seat-aisle: version 1, provenance {'source': 'chat', 'thread': 'thread-2'}

2. A near duplicate is skipped, and confirms the memory it repeats
   reconcile seat-aisle-again: skipped, confirmed ['seat-aisle']
   seat-aisle is confirmed 1 time

3. A fact that arrives late goes straight into history
   reconcile seat-window-2025, true as of 2025-03-01: superseded
   live memories in the seat slot: ['seat-aisle']

4. History keeps each old version, why it ended and where it came from
   seat-window, version 1: 'I prefer window seats.'
      true from 2026-01-15 to 2026-10-29, superseded by seat-aisle, provenance {'source': 'chat', 'thread': 'thread-1'}
   seat-window-2025, version 1: 'I prefer window seats.'
      true from 2025-03-01 to 2026-10-29, superseded by seat-aisle, provenance {'source': 'chat', 'thread': 'thread-2025-03'}

5. Two steps: find_conflicts, a judge decides, resolve applies the decision
   find_conflicts no-peanut-allergy: allergy (similar, score 0.90): 'Allergic to peanuts.'
   judge: ['supersede allergy']
   meanwhile, another writer puts allergy again
   resolve: ConflictsChanged for ['allergy'], so find them again
   find_conflicts no-peanut-allergy: allergy (similar, score 0.90): 'Allergic to peanuts and cashews.'
   resolve: written, version 1, superseded ['allergy']

6. confirm renews a memory's expiry, for longer each time it is confirmed
   seat-aisle: confirmed 1 time, expires in 30 days
   confirm: True, confirmed 2 times, expires in 60 days
   confirm: True, confirmed 3 times, expires in 120 days
   confirm a memory that does not exist: False

7. Two writers update one memory with record() and put_if()
   put_if airlines, expected=None: applied, version 1
   again: conflict, the current memory is version 1
   both writers read version 1
   writer 1 adds Iberia: applied, version 2
   writer 2 adds KLM: conflict, the current memory is version 2
   writer 2 adds KLM: applied, version 3
   airlines, version 3: ['Iberia', 'KLM', 'TAP']

8. Forgetting: delete keeps history, purge removes the memory and its history
   delete airlines: get gives None, history [(3, 'deleted'), (2, 'overwritten'), (1, 'overwritten')]
   purge airlines: True, history now []
   purge seat-window: True, history now []

The dates in step 4 depend on the day you run it: the aisle preference is true from when it was written.

docs.title: The Async Version
docs.text: AsyncCockroachDBStore has each of these methods as a coroutine with an a prefix: areconcile, afind_conflicts, aresolve, arecord, aconfirm, aput_if, adelete_if, ahistory and apurge. The policies and the TTL function stay plain functions.
