docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Learn how to configure langchain-cockroachdb for different workloads.

For an existing virtualized deployment, see Virtual-cluster connections. On a self-hosted cluster the application virtual cluster is selected with the percent-encoded options=-ccluster%3Dmain. The unencoded options=-ccluster=main that the CockroachDB docs show for cockroach sql is rejected by psycopg/libpq (extra key/value separator "=" in URI query parameter: "options"); only SQLAlchemy accepts it.

docs.title: Basic Configuration
docs.text:
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBEngine

engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(
    "cockroachdb://user:pass@host:26257/db",
    pool_size=10,  # Base connections
    max_overflow=20,  # Additional connections
    pool_pre_ping=True,  # Health check before use
    pool_recycle=3600,  # Recycle after 1 hour
    pool_timeout=30.0,  # Wait 30s for connection
    connect_timeout=10,  # Connection timeout (default: 10)
)

docs.title: Retry Configuration
docs.text:
Set a RetryPolicy on the engine to control which errors are retried and how:

from langchain_cockroachdb import (
    AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore,
    CockroachDBChatMessageHistory,
    CockroachDBEngine,
    RetryPolicy,
)

engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(
    "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable",
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=8, max_backoff=5.0),
)
store = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(engine, embeddings, "documents")  # inherits
history = CockroachDBChatMessageHistory("session-1", engine=engine)  # inherits
fast_store = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine, embeddings, "documents", retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=2)
)

See Retries and Resilience for what is retried and every option.

docs.title: Basic Settings
docs.text:
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore

vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine=engine,
    embeddings=embeddings,
    collection_name="documents",
    # Column names
    content_column="content",
    embedding_column="embedding",
    metadata_column="metadata",
    id_column="id",
    # Distance metric
    distance_strategy=DistanceStrategy.COSINE,  # or L2, IP
    # Batch size for inserts
    batch_size=100,
)

docs.title: Retry Settings
docs.text:
The vector store inherits the engine's retry policy. Each insert batch is retried on its own. Override the policy with retry_policy or shorthand retry_* arguments:

vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine=engine,
    embeddings=embeddings,
    collection_name="documents",
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3, max_backoff=5.0),
)

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
# Optimized for local development
engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(
    connection_string,
    pool_size=5,
    max_overflow=10,
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3, max_backoff=1.0),
)

vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine=engine,
    embeddings=embeddings,
    collection_name="docs",
    batch_size=100,

engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(
    connection_string,
    pool_size=20,
    max_overflow=40,
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=10, max_backoff=30.0),
)

vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine=engine,
    embeddings=embeddings,
    collection_name="docs",
    batch_size=100,
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=5),
)

docs.title: Batch Jobs
docs.text:
# Resilient, patient retries
engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(
    connection_string,
    pool_size=3,
    max_overflow=5,
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=20, max_backoff=60.0),
)

vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine=engine,
    embeddings=embeddings,
    collection_name="docs",
    batch_size=500,  # Larger batches for throughput
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=10),
)

docs.title: Multi-Region
docs.text:
from langchain_cockroachdb import RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES, RetryPolicy

# Tolerates failovers and high latency
failover = RetryPolicy(
    max_attempts=8,
    max_backoff=5.0,
    retryable_sqlstates=RETRYABLE_SQLSTATES | {"57014"},
    attempt_timeout=10,
)

    connection_string,
    pool_size=15,
    max_overflow=30,
    pool_timeout=60.0,  # Longer timeout

Workload Type pool_size max_overflow Development 5 10 Web (low traffic) 10 20 Web (high traffic) 20-50 40-100 Batch jobs 3-5 5-10 Analytics 10-20 20-40

docs.title: Basic Vector Store Example
docs.text:
import asyncio
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore, CockroachDBEngine
from langchain_core.embeddings import DeterministicFakeEmbedding

async def main():
    # 1. Create engine
    engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(
        "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"
    )

    # 2. Initialize table
    await engine.ainit_vectorstore_table(
        table_name="my_documents",
        vector_dimension=384,
        drop_if_exists=True,
    )

    # 3. Create vector store
    embeddings = DeterministicFakeEmbedding(size=384)
    vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
        engine=engine,
        embeddings=embeddings,
        collection_name="my_documents",
    )

    # 4. Add documents
    texts = [
        "CockroachDB is a distributed SQL database",
        "LangChain simplifies building LLM applications",
        "Vector search enables semantic similarity",
    ]
    ids = await vectorstore.aadd_texts(texts)
    print(f"Added {len(ids)} documents")

    # 5. Search
    results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(
        "Tell me about databases",
        k=2
    )

    for doc in results:
        print(f"- {doc.page_content}")

    # 6. Cleanup
    await engine.aclose()

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Async vs Sync Guide
docs.text: Understanding when to use async and sync APIs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: langchain-cockroachdb provides both async and sync interfaces: - Async (recommended): High-performance, I/O concurrency - Sync: Simple wrapper for scripts and batch jobs

docs.title: How Sync Methods Run
docs.text:
Sync methods run their database work on one background event loop, so they are safe from any number of threads and from inside a running event loop. Use one style per engine; the engine logs a warning if it sees both at the same time. Engines that use the built-in background loop are also safe across os.fork(): a child process gets a fresh pool and loop.

An engine built with loop= (CockroachDBEngine(engine, loop=...) or CockroachDBEngine.from_engine(engine, loop=...)) sends its sync calls, and async calls from other event loops, to that loop. Keep the loop running in its thread while the engine is in use. If the loop is closed, is not running, or stops while a call waits on it, the call raises RuntimeError instead of waiting forever. A loop that is not running gets about a second to start, or to start again, before calls give up. When a call gives up after its work started, the work may or may not have taken effect. The library's writes are safe to retry (see the resilience guide). The loop's thread does not survive os.fork(), so in a child process such an engine raises RuntimeError too, and so does a new engine built there on a loop that was running in the parent. Build a new engine in the child, with a loop started in the child, or without loop=.

docs.title: Quick Comparison
docs.text: Feature Async Sync Throughput High (100-1000+ req/s) Low (10-50 req/s) I/O Handling Non-blocking Blocking Concurrency Native Limited Code Style async/await Regular Python Best For Web apps, APIs, high load Scripts, batch jobs, simple tools

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
✅ Web Applications 

# FastAPI, Django Async, etc.
from fastapi import FastAPI
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/search")
async def search(query: str):
    results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(query, k=5)
    return results

✅ High Concurrent Load 

# Handle 100s of requests simultaneously
async def handle_many_requests(queries: list[str]):
    tasks = [
        vectorstore.asimilarity_search(q, k=5) 
        for q in queries
    ]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    return results

✅ Modern LLM APIs 

# OpenAI, Anthropic APIs are async
async def rag_pipeline(query: str):
    # Vector search (async)
    docs = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(query, k=5)

    # LLM call (async)
    response = await llm.ainvoke(docs)

    return response

✅ Streaming Applications 

async def stream_results(query: str):
    async for doc in vectorstore.astream_search(query):
        yield doc

docs.text: All methods prefixed with a: - aadd_texts() - Add documents - aadd_documents() - Add document objects - asimilarity_search() - Search - asimilarity_search_with_score() - Search with scores - adelete() - Delete documents - aapply_vector_index() - Create index - adrop_vector_index() - Drop index

✅ Simple Scripts

docs.text: Same names without a prefix: - add_texts() - Add documents - add_documents() - Add document objects - similarity_search() - Search - similarity_search_with_score() - Search with scores - delete() - Delete documents - apply_vector_index() - Create index - drop_vector_index() - Drop index

docs.title: Throughput Test
docs.text:
Async: 

async def async_benchmark():
    # 100 concurrent searches
    queries = ["query"] * 100
    start = time.time()

    tasks = [
        vectorstore.asimilarity_search(q, k=5) 
        for q in queries
    ]
    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Async: {100/elapsed:.0f} queries/sec")

# Result: ~800 queries/sec

Sync: 

def sync_benchmark():
    # 100 sequential searches
    queries = ["query"] * 100
    start = time.time()

    for q in queries:
        vectorstore.similarity_search(q, k=5)

    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Sync: {100/elapsed:.0f} queries/sec")

# Result: ~40 queries/sec

Result: Async is 20x faster for concurrent operations.

docs.title: Why Async is Faster
docs.text:
Sync (blocking): 

Query 1: [DB wait] [process] ────┐
Query 2:                          [DB wait] [process] ────┐
Query 3:                                                  [DB wait] [process]
Total: 300ms

Async (non-blocking): 

Query 1: [DB wait] [process]
Query 2: [DB wait] [process]
Query 3: [DB wait] [process]
         ▲ All waiting simultaneously
Total: 100ms

docs.title: Async Function with Sync Wrapper
docs.text:
# Define async logic
async def complex_rag_pipeline(query: str) -> str:
    docs = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(query, k=5)
    response = await llm.ainvoke(docs)
    return response.content

# Provide sync wrapper for simple use
def rag(query: str) -> str:
    """Sync wrapper for RAG pipeline."""
    return asyncio.run(complex_rag_pipeline(query))

# Use sync wrapper in scripts
result = rag("What is CockroachDB?")
print(result)

docs.title: Data Migration Script
docs.text:
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBVectorStore

def migrate_documents(source_file: str):
    """Simple sync script for one-time migration."""
    vectorstore = CockroachDBVectorStore(
        engine=engine,
        embeddings=embeddings,
        collection_name="docs",
    )

    # Read documents
    with open(source_file) as f:
        docs = f.readlines()

    # Process in batches
    batch_size = 100
    for i in range(0, len(docs), batch_size):
        batch = docs[i:i+batch_size]
        ids = vectorstore.add_texts(batch)
        print(f"Migrated batch {i//batch_size + 1}: {len(ids)} docs")

# Run
migrate_documents("documents.txt")

    await vectorstore.aadd_texts(["doc1"])
    results = vectorstore.similarity_search("query", k=5)  # Wrong!

    docs = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(query, k=5)
    response = await llm.ainvoke(docs)
    await log_to_db(query, response)

docs.title: 4. Close Connections Properly
docs.text:
# Async
try:
    await vectorstore.aadd_texts(texts)
finally:
    await engine.aclose()

# Sync
try:
    vectorstore.add_texts(texts)
finally:
    engine.close()

docs.title: "RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop"
docs.text:
You're trying to use asyncio.run() inside an async function:

# Wrong
async def my_function():
    result = asyncio.run(vectorstore.asimilarity_search("query"))

# Right
async def my_function():
    result = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search("query")

docs.title: Slow Performance with Sync API
docs.text:
Consider switching to async if you have: - Multiple concurrent operations - I/O-bound workload - Web application with many users

# Before (slow)
for query in queries:
    vectorstore.similarity_search(query, k=5)

# After (fast)
async def process_queries(queries):
    tasks = [
        vectorstore.asimilarity_search(q, k=5) 
        for q in queries
    ]
    return await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

docs.title: With LCEL Chains
docs.text:
from langchain_core.runnables.history import RunnableWithMessageHistory
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate, MessagesPlaceholder
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

# Define prompt
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You are a helpful assistant."),
    MessagesPlaceholder(variable_name="history"),
    ("human", "{input}"),
])

# Create chain
chain = prompt | ChatOpenAI()

# Wrap with message history
chain_with_history = RunnableWithMessageHistory(
    chain,
    lambda session_id: CockroachDBChatMessageHistory(
        session_id=session_id,
        connection_string=connection_string,
    ),
    input_messages_key="input",
    history_messages_key="history",
)

# Use with session
response = chain_with_history.invoke(
    {"input": "Hello!"},
    config={"configurable": {"session_id": "user-123"}},
)
print(response.content)

from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBEngine, CockroachDBChatMessageHistory

from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBChatMessageHistory
from langchain.memory import ConversationBufferMemory
from langchain.chains import ConversationChain
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

def create_chatbot(user_id: str):
    """Create chatbot with persistent history."""
    history = CockroachDBChatMessageHistory(
        session_id=f"user-{user_id}",
        connection_string=connection_string,
    )

    memory = ConversationBufferMemory(
        chat_memory=history,
        return_messages=True,
    )

    return ConversationChain(
        llm=ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4"),
        memory=memory,
    )

# Use chatbot
bot = create_chatbot("user-123")

# First conversation
response1 = bot.predict(input="My name is Alice")

docs.title: Multi-Turn Dialog

async def handle_conversation(user_id: str, messages: list[str]):
    """Process multi-turn conversation."""
    history = CockroachDBChatMessageHistory(
        session_id=f"user-{user_id}",
        connection_string=connection_string,
    )

    llm = ChatOpenAI()

    for user_msg in messages:
        # Add user message
        history.add_user_message(user_msg)

        # Get context
        context = history.messages

        # Generate response
        response = await llm.ainvoke(context)

        # Save AI response
        history.add_ai_message(response.content)

        print(f"User: {user_msg}")
        print(f"AI: {response.content}\n")

# Use
await handle_conversation("user-123", [
    "Hello!",
    "What can you help me with?",
    "Tell me about CockroachDB",
])

docs.title: LangGraph Checkpointer Guide
docs.text: Persist LangGraph workflow state in CockroachDB for short-term memory, human-in-the-loop patterns, and fault-tolerant agent execution.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The CockroachDB checkpointer provides:

  • Short-term memory for multi-turn conversations in LangGraph agents
  • Human-in-the-loop support with interrupt/resume capabilities
  • Fault tolerance with persistent state across process restarts
  • Distributed durability backed by CockroachDB's transaction isolation (SERIALIZABLE default, READ COMMITTED also supported)

The implementation mirrors langgraph-checkpoint-postgres with adaptations for CockroachDB compatibility.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install langchain-cockroachdb

The checkpointer requires langgraph-checkpoint>=2.1.2 and psycopg[binary]>=3.0.0, which are included as dependencies.

docs.title: Synchronous Usage
docs.text:
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver

DB_URI = "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"

with CockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as checkpointer:
    checkpointer.setup()

    # Compile your LangGraph workflow with the checkpointer
    graph = workflow.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

    # Invoke with a thread_id for persistent state
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-123"}}
    result = graph.invoke({"messages": [("user", "Hello!")]}, config)

    # Continue the conversation -- state is persisted
    result = graph.invoke({"messages": [("user", "What did I just say?")]}, config)

docs.title: Asynchronous Usage
docs.text:
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBSaver

DB_URI = "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"

async with AsyncCockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as checkpointer:
    await checkpointer.setup()

    graph = workflow.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-456"}}
    result = await graph.ainvoke({"messages": [("user", "Hello!")]}, config)

docs.title: Direct Connection
docs.text:
Best for scripts or single-process applications:

from psycopg import Connection
from psycopg.rows import dict_row
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver

conn = Connection.connect(
    "postgresql://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable",
    autocommit=True,
    prepare_threshold=5,
    row_factory=dict_row,
)
saver = CockroachDBSaver(conn)
saver.setup()

Note

Use postgresql:// (not cockroachdb://) when creating raw psycopg connections directly. The from_conn_string() factory handles this conversion automatically.

docs.title: Connection Pool
docs.text:
Best for web applications and high-concurrency workloads. A saver on a pool runs operations concurrently, each on its own pooled connection, so one saver can serve many agents, threads or tasks. A saver on a single connection runs operations one at a time, so long-running services should use a pool. A shared pooled saver runs as many operations at once as the pool has connections, so set max_size for the number of agents you expect to run at the same time. psycopg_pool's default max_size equals min_size, which defaults to 4. When every connection is busy, an operation waits up to the pool's timeout and then raises PoolTimeout, which is not retried. For example:

from psycopg_pool import ConnectionPool
from psycopg.rows import dict_row
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver

pool = ConnectionPool(
    "postgresql://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable",
    max_size=20,
    kwargs={"autocommit": True, "row_factory": dict_row},
)
saver = CockroachDBSaver(pool)
saver.setup()

docs.title: Async Connection Pool
docs.text:
from psycopg_pool import AsyncConnectionPool
from psycopg.rows import dict_row
from langchain_cockroachdb import AsyncCockroachDBSaver

pool = AsyncConnectionPool(
    "postgresql://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable",
    max_size=20,
    kwargs={"autocommit": True, "row_factory": dict_row},
)
saver = AsyncCockroachDBSaver(pool)
await saver.setup()

Pools you build yourself do not get the library's gssencmode=disable default. On macOS with prefork servers, add gssencmode=disable to the pool's conninfo or kwargs.

docs.title: Factory Method (Recommended)
docs.text:
The simplest approach -- handles connection string conversion, pool setup, and enables prepared statement caching (prepare_threshold=5) for query plan reuse:

# Sync
with CockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string("cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb") as saver:
    saver.setup()

# Async
async with AsyncCockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string("cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb") as saver:
    await saver.setup()

docs.title: Retries and Connection Pools
docs.text:
A single connection cannot recover once it drops, so the savers do not retry a dead single connection. Give them a pool, which replaces broken connections:

from psycopg.rows import dict_row
from psycopg_pool import ConnectionPool

from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver, RetryPolicy

with ConnectionPool(
    "postgresql://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable",
    kwargs={"autocommit": True, "row_factory": dict_row},
    open=True,
) as pool:
    checkpointer = CockroachDBSaver(pool, retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=8))
    checkpointer.setup()  # safe to run from several processes at once

A pipelined saver (from_conn_string(..., pipeline=True)) uses one connection, so it also cannot recover once that connection drops. Use a pool for long-running services.

setup() is safe to run from several processes at once and resumes where it stopped if it is interrupted.

from_conn_string accepts retry_policy, connect_timeout, prepare_threshold and connect_kwargs (for example {"application_name": "my-service"}).

docs.title: Saving Checkpoints
docs.text:
Checkpoints are saved automatically by LangGraph during graph execution. You can also save manually:

from langgraph.checkpoint.base import empty_checkpoint

config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "my-thread", "checkpoint_ns": ""}}
checkpoint = empty_checkpoint()
metadata = {"source": "input", "step": 1}

saved_config = saver.put(config, checkpoint, metadata, {})

docs.title: Retrieving Checkpoints
docs.text:
# Get the latest checkpoint for a thread
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "my-thread", "checkpoint_ns": ""}}
result = saver.get_tuple(config)

if result:
    print(result.checkpoint)   # The checkpoint data
    print(result.metadata)     # Associated metadata
    print(result.config)       # Config with actual checkpoint_id

docs.title: Listing Checkpoints
docs.text:
# List all checkpoints (across all threads)
for checkpoint_tuple in saver.list(None):
    print(checkpoint_tuple.config)

# Filter by thread
thread_config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "my-thread"}}
for checkpoint_tuple in saver.list(thread_config):
    print(checkpoint_tuple.metadata)

# Filter by metadata
for checkpoint_tuple in saver.list(None, filter={"source": "loop"}):
    print(checkpoint_tuple.config)

# Limit results
for checkpoint_tuple in saver.list(None, limit=5):
    print(checkpoint_tuple.config)

docs.title: Deleting Threads
docs.text: saver.delete_thread("my-thread")

docs.title: Storing Intermediate Writes
docs.text: saver.put_writes(config, [("channel_name", value)], task_id="task-1")

docs.title: Atomic Writes
docs.text:
put with channel blobs, put_writes with several writes, and delete_thread send BEGIN, their statements and COMMIT as one batch, so each write is saved completely or not at all, even when the caller is cancelled or fails partway. A write still takes one round trip, and CockroachDB can still retry it on the server. Single-statement writes are unchanged.

On a single connection that the caller also uses, a write made inside a transaction the caller opened joins it as a savepoint, so the caller's commit or rollback decides. The saver never rolls back a transaction it did not open, and an error inside the caller's transaction is raised at once, without retries, so the caller's own retry loop can restart the whole transaction.

docs.title: Chatbot with Memory
docs.text:
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START, END
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver

DB_URI = "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"

llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")


def chatbot(state: MessagesState):
    return {"messages": [llm.invoke(state["messages"])]}


graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)
graph.add_node("chatbot", chatbot)
graph.add_edge(START, "chatbot")
graph.add_edge("chatbot", END)

with CockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as checkpointer:
    checkpointer.setup()
    app = graph.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)

    # First turn
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "session-1"}}
    result = app.invoke(
        {"messages": [("user", "My name is Alice")]},
        config,
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)

    # Second turn -- the bot remembers the name
    result = app.invoke(
        {"messages": [("user", "What is my name?")]},
        config,
    )
    print(result["messages"][-1].content)

docs.title: Human-in-the-Loop
docs.text:
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.base import empty_checkpoint
from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBSaver

DB_URI = "cockroachdb://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb?sslmode=disable"


def step_1(state: MessagesState):
    return {"messages": [("assistant", "Ready for approval")]}


def step_2(state: MessagesState):
    return {"messages": [("assistant", "Approved and executed")]}


graph = StateGraph(MessagesState)
graph.add_node("step_1", step_1)
graph.add_node("step_2", step_2)
graph.add_edge(START, "step_1")
graph.add_edge("step_1", "step_2")
graph.add_edge("step_2", END)

with CockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as checkpointer:
    checkpointer.setup()
    app = graph.compile(
        checkpointer=checkpointer,
        interrupt_before=["step_2"],
    )

    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "approval-1"}}

    # Runs step_1 then pauses before step_2
    result = app.invoke(
        {"messages": [("user", "Start workflow")]},
        config,
    )
    print("Paused for approval:", result["messages"][-1])

    # Resume after human approval
    result = app.invoke(None, config)
    print("Completed:", result["messages"][-1])

docs.title: Crash Recovery and Durability Modes
docs.text:
LangGraph decides when a checkpoint is written through the durability argument of invoke, stream and their async versions. See LangGraph's durability modes.

  • "sync": each checkpoint is written before the next step starts.
  • "async": each checkpoint is written in the background while the next step runs. This is LangGraph's default.
  • "exit": state is written only when the run ends.

With "async", a process that dies shortly after a step can lose that step's checkpoint, and with it the record of a tool call the model made. After a restart the graph resumes from an older checkpoint, so the model can plan the same call again under a new tool-call ID. An idempotency key built from the tool-call ID does not catch that repeat, because the ID it was built from was never saved.

When a crash between steps matters, for example when tools charge cards, send messages or change other systems, pass durability="sync":

result = app.invoke(inputs, config, durability="sync")

"sync" adds a write to CockroachDB before each step. Keep "async" where losing the last step is acceptable, such as a chat turn the user can repeat.

Even with "sync", a node that was interrupted or did not finish runs again from its first line when the graph resumes, so a tool that reached an external service before the crash can run twice. Make such tools idempotent. Derive a key from state that was saved before the tool ran, such as the thread ID and the tool-call ID, and have the receiving service ignore a repeated key and return the original result.

docs.title: Application-process Recovery
docs.text: For application-crash recovery coverage, see the process-recovery tests. They validate approval resume and pending-write reuse with a fresh process and pool, using durability="sync" on both sync and async graph calls. On Python 3.10, approval resume works only with the sync API, because an async graph's interrupt() needs Python 3.11 or newer. Interrupted or unfinished nodes can execute code again, so external tool effects need application-level idempotency or reconciliation.

docs.title: Schema and Migrations
docs.text:
The setup() method creates three tables and associated indexes:

Table Purpose checkpoints Stores checkpoint data and metadata per thread/namespace checkpoint_blobs Stores serialized channel values (binary blobs) checkpoint_writes Stores intermediate writes for pending sends

Migrations are applied incrementally and idempotently -- calling setup() multiple times is safe.

docs.title: Row-Level TTL
docs.text: CockroachDB supports automatic deletion of expired rows via Row-Level TTL. The checkpointer exposes this as an opt-in feature for automatic cleanup of old checkpoint data.

docs.title: Enabling TTL
docs.text:
# Sync
with CockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as saver:
    saver.setup()

    # Expire threads idle for 30 days, clean up daily
    saver.enable_ttl(ttl_interval="30 days", cron="@daily")

# Async
async with AsyncCockroachDBSaver.from_conn_string(DB_URI) as saver:
    await saver.setup()
    await saver.aenable_ttl(ttl_interval="7 days", cron="@hourly")

docs.title: Disabling TTL
docs.text:
saver.disable_ttl()       # sync
await saver.adisable_ttl()  # async

docs.title: What TTL Expires
docs.text:
Each row expires by its own created_at, which setup() adds to all three tables with DEFAULT now().

  • A checkpoint row, and the writes saved with it, expire ttl_interval after they were written. The older checkpoints of an active thread expire too, so its history gets shorter while its latest checkpoints stay.
  • A blob row holds one channel's value at one version. It is written once, when the channel changes, and every later checkpoint in which the channel kept that version uses the same row. A blob row expires ttl_interval plus a tenth of it after its created_at.

enable_ttl() stores months and years as days, 30 to a month and 365 to a year, so "1 month" is stored as "30 days". CockroachDB adds months and years by the calendar, and the same month added on two days a little apart can differ by up to 3 days, which no grace of a tenth could cover. An interval of fixed length keeps the guarantees below exact.

A channel that has not changed since an early step, such as a profile set on the first turn, keeps its first blob row. So while TTL is on, each put brings created_at forward to now on the blob rows its checkpoint uses but does not write, once they are older than a tenth of the interval. It does this in the same transaction as the checkpoint row. The extra tenth is the grace: after a put, each blob row the new checkpoint uses expires no earlier than the checkpoint.

Puts only cover threads that write, and only once their saver knows that TTL is on. So when enable_ttl() turns TTL on or changes it, it does four things:

  1. It writes the new settings with TTL paused (ttl_pause): they are in place, but CockroachDB's TTL job deletes nothing.
  2. It waits TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS (10 seconds) plus TTL_PAUSE_MARGIN_SECONDS (5 seconds), about 15 seconds, so that every saver reads the new setting and the puts already under way finish. If the retry policy's attempt_timeout is longer than the margin, it waits that instead of the margin, since one attempt can last that long. Savers refresh while TTL is paused, so from then on every put refreshes. One narrow case remains: a put that decided before the wait, and took longer than the margin to commit, counting any wait for a pooled connection, can miss its refresh. A thread that writes that way and then stays idle can lose a blob row the pass left alone. Changing the setting when few threads are active avoids it.
  3. It makes one pass over the checkpoints. For each blob row that the checkpoints inside the interval use, it finds the newest of those checkpoints. If the row is older than that checkpoint by more than a tenth of the interval, the pass brings its created_at forward to now. So threads that are idle keep their state too.
  4. It reads the setting of checkpoint_blobs again and resumes TTL, checkpoint_blobs last. If another run has written a different setting meanwhile, it leaves TTL paused for that run to resume, and logs that at INFO.

Only rows left unchanged that long are rewritten, so the pass does not rewrite the table: the messages a thread changes every step have rows that only their own checkpoints use. The pass reads every checkpoint once, TTL_REFRESH_BATCH_SIZE (500) at a time, and changes at most TTL_REFRESH_UPDATE_SIZE (100) rows per UPDATE. Each read and each UPDATE is its own short statement, retried on its own under the retry policy's ddl_attempt_timeout. enable_ttl() logs at INFO when it pauses TTL, when the pass starts and ends, with the number of blob rows it brought forward, and when it resumes TTL.

So whenever the setting changes, enable_ttl() blocks for about 15 seconds on a table of any size, plus the time the pass takes. That includes the first call after upgrading from 0.5. Called again with the same setting in place and running, it returns at once, after updating the cron. Any other change makes the whole run, a longer interval too: TTL deletes expired rows only when its job gets to them, so a longer interval can bring back checkpoints whose blob rows the old setting had already expired. If your processes call enable_ttl() as they start and their startup probes are tight, run it once from a single process or a one-off job before the rollout. The calls they then make find the same setting in place and return at once.

Use one interval in every process, and change it from one process. If two runs with different intervals overlap, each resumes TTL only if its own setting is still in place, so the run that wrote last resumes it.

After TTL resumes, CockroachDB may skip its next scheduled TTL job once, with "found a recent schema change". That delays deletion by one cron period.

A run that stops before it resumes TTL leaves it paused, which deletes nothing. A run that stops during the resume statements leaves only checkpoint_blobs paused, since it resumes last. Then checkpoints and writes expire again while blob rows stay, which only leaves behind blob rows that no checkpoint uses. Either way, run enable_ttl() again: it takes a paused setting for a run that did not finish, so it waits, makes the pass and resumes TTL, even with the same interval. While TTL is paused, CockroachDB's scheduled TTL job fails with "ttl jobs on table ... are currently paused" and deletes nothing. A saver that finds TTL on checkpoint_blobs paused logs a WARNING, once per process each time it is paused. It says that TTL deletes nothing while paused, and that if no enable_ttl() run is under way, one stopped before it finished, so run enable_ttl() again. Savers log it during a run too. enable_ttl() cannot tell how a setting in place got there, so after a setting written by hand or with copied DDL, or data imported while TTL was on, call disable_ttl() and then enable_ttl() to make it run the pass.

So once enable_ttl() has run, a thread keeps its whole state while it is active, and expires once it has been idle for ttl_interval. A blob row that no checkpoint uses any more stays at most a tenth of the interval longer than the checkpoints did. A row that the pass in enable_ttl() brought forward can stay up to about one interval longer than its thread, once. While TTL is on, a put that uses blob rows it does not write sends one more UPDATE in its transaction, and a blob row is rewritten at most once per tenth of the interval.

The saver learns whether TTL is on, and the interval, from the settings of checkpoint_blobs in the catalog. It reads them on the first put that needs them and keeps them for TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS (10 seconds), counted from when the read started, so it sees a change another process makes within 10 seconds. That is at most one small catalog read per saver every 10 seconds, made only by puts that use blob rows they do not write. Each attempt of a put decides again whether to refresh, so a retry made after the saver learns that TTL is on refreshes too. Its own enable_ttl() and disable_ttl() take effect for it at once. enable_ttl() waits its own saver's TTL_STATE_CACHE_SECONDS for every saver, so keep that value the same in every process. If the read fails with a database error that the retry policy does not retry, such as a missing privilege, puts go on without the refresh, the saver logs a WARNING once, and it reads again after the cache interval.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• enable_ttl() uses CockroachDB's ttl_expiration_expression, which avoids the full table rewrite that ttl_expire_after causes.
  • CockroachDB runs a background job on the cron schedule. It deletes checkpoint and write rows whose created_at + interval has passed, and blob rows whose created_at + interval + interval / 10 has.
  • enable_ttl() is idempotent. Calling it again updates the interval and cron.
  • enable_ttl() refuses an interval longer than 106,751 days, about 292 years. That is the longest duration CockroachDB keeps, and the pass binds the interval as one.
  • disable_ttl() removes TTL from all three tables, a pause included.
  • A TTL setting on checkpoint_blobs that enable_ttl() did not write, such as one set by hand, turns the refresh off. The saver logs that at INFO, once per process.

Note

TTL deletion is eventual: expired rows remain queryable until the background job runs. CockroachDB rate-limits deletions to minimize impact on foreground queries.

docs.title: Upgrading from 0.5
docs.text: In 0.5, blob rows got no grace, puts did not refresh them, and months and years were stored as written. After upgrading, run enable_ttl() once more with the same interval and cron. It adds the grace, stores months and years as days, and brings forward the blob rows of threads that have been idle since the upgrade, pausing TTL while it does. It blocks for about 15 seconds plus the pass, so if startup probes are tight, run it once from a single process or a one-off job before the rollout. Until then, puts refresh blob rows, but with the 0.5 setting a thread that has written since the upgrade can lose blob rows up to a tenth of the interval before its last checkpoint expires, and a thread idle since the upgrade up to the whole interval before. A 0.5 setting in months or years is still read for the refresh, but only approximately.

docs.title: Graphs with DeltaChannel
docs.text:
LangGraph's DeltaChannel, which Deep Agents uses for its messages and files, stores each step's change and a full snapshot only every so many steps. To load the state, the saver rebuilds such a channel from older checkpoints and their writes, back to the last snapshot. TTL still expires those older checkpoints by age, even while the thread is active. So for these graphs, pick a TTL longer than a thread stays active, or delete finished threads with delete_thread().

When the history of a delta channel stops at a missing checkpoint before its snapshot, get_delta_channel_history logs a WARNING. It names the thread, its checkpoint_ns and the missing checkpoint, and says that the state of those channels may be incomplete. A saver logs each missing checkpoint once. What it returns is unchanged.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The CockroachDB checkpointer includes several performance optimizations over the base PostgresSaver approach:

docs.title: Separate Lightweight Queries
docs.text: Instead of correlated subqueries with jsonb_agg/jsonb_build_object, the checkpointer issues separate simple queries for checkpoints, blobs, and writes. Each query uses primary key lookups.

docs.title: Batch Fetching in list()
docs.text: When listing multiple checkpoints, blobs and writes for all returned checkpoints are fetched in just 2 batch queries (instead of 2 per checkpoint). This reduces database round trips from 2N+1 to 3 total, regardless of how many checkpoints are returned.

docs.title: Raw BYTEA Deserialization
docs.text: Blob data is read as raw BYTEA via psycopg3's binary cursor protocol, eliminating the overhead of hex-encoding in SQL and decoding in Python.

docs.title: Prepared Statement Caching
docs.text:
The from_conn_string() factory sets prepare_threshold=5 by default, enabling server-side prepared statement caching after 5 executions of the same query. This eliminates repeated query parsing and planning overhead for hot paths. prepare_threshold is configurable via from_conn_string(prepare_threshold=...), and None turns prepared statements off.

Statements sent in a pipeline are never prepared: the writes (put, put_writes, delete_thread) and, with pipeline=True, every statement. In pipeline mode psycopg records a statement as prepared before the server confirms it. If an earlier statement in the same batch fails, the server never prepares it, and later runs on that connection could fail with "prepared statement ... does not exist".

docs.title: CockroachDB-Specific Adaptations
docs.text: This checkpointer is modeled on langgraph-checkpoint-postgres (PostgresSaver) with the following adaptations for CockroachDB compatibility:

docs.title: Separate Queries Instead of Multidimensional Arrays
docs.text: CockroachDB does not support multidimensional arrays. The PostgresSaver uses correlated subqueries with array_agg(array[...]). The CockroachDB checkpointer instead fetches blobs and writes via separate lightweight primary key lookups, with batch variants for list().

docs.title: Index Creation Without CONCURRENTLY
docs.text: CockroachDB creates indexes in a non-blocking manner by default, so the CONCURRENTLY keyword used by PostgresSaver is omitted.

docs.title: Connection String Sanitization
docs.text: The from_conn_string() factory automatically converts cockroachdb:// URLs to postgresql:// for psycopg compatibility.

docs.title: Explicit Table Function Aliases
docs.text:
CockroachDB requires explicit aliases for set-returning functions like jsonb_each_text():

-- Required for CockroachDB:
FROM jsonb_each_text(checkpoint -> 'channel_versions') AS jt
-- Not: FROM jsonb_each_text(checkpoint -> 'channel_versions')

docs.title: Comparison with PostgresSaver
docs.text: Feature PostgresSaver CockroachDBSaver Connection library psycopg3 psycopg3 Connection modes Connection, Pool, Pipeline Connection, Pool, Pipeline Isolation level READ COMMITTED SERIALIZABLE (default), READ COMMITTED supported Blob/write fetching Correlated subqueries Separate PK lookups + batch fetching Index creation CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY CREATE INDEX (non-blocking by default) Blob encoding Native bytea arrays Raw BYTEA via binary cursor Prepared statements prepare_threshold=0 (each query from its first run) prepare_threshold=5 (after five runs, outside pipelines) Row-level TTL Not supported enable_ttl() / disable_ttl() Async support Yes Yes Thread deletion Yes Yes Pipeline support Yes Yes

docs.title: Hybrid Search Guide
docs.text: Combine full-text search with vector similarity for better retrieval.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Hybrid search runs two searches for every query and merges the results:

  • Full-text search (FTS): keyword matching over a TSVECTOR column using ts_rank
  • Vector search: semantic similarity over embeddings
  • Score fusion: the two ranked lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion or a weighted sum

Both searches run in parallel, so the latency cost over a plain vector search is small.

Benefits:

  • Better recall: exact keywords and semantic matches both surface
  • Robust to query formulation
  • Keyword-only matches that vector search would miss still come back as full documents

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Hybrid search needs a tsvector column and GIN index on the table. Create the table with create_tsvector=True and pass a HybridSearchConfig to the store:

from langchain_cockroachdb import (
    AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore,
    CockroachDBEngine,
    HybridSearchConfig,
)

engine = CockroachDBEngine.from_connection_string(connection_string)

# create_tsvector=True adds the tsvector column and GIN index
await engine.ainit_vectorstore_table(
    table_name="documents",
    vector_dimension=1536,
    create_tsvector=True,
)

vectorstore = AsyncCockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine=engine,
    embeddings=embeddings,
    collection_name="documents",
    hybrid_search_config=HybridSearchConfig(),
)

Behind the scenes the table gets:

ALTER TABLE documents
ADD COLUMN content_tsvector TSVECTOR
GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', content)) STORED;

CREATE INDEX ON documents USING GIN (content_tsvector);

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
Once the config is set, the normal search methods do hybrid search transparently. There is no separate hybrid method to call:

# Runs FTS and vector search in parallel, fuses, returns top k
results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(
    "distributed databases performance", k=10
)

for doc in results:
    print(doc.page_content)

With scores (these are fused scores, not raw distances):

results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search_with_score(
    "CockroachDB scalability", k=10
)

for doc, score in results:
    print(f"{score:.4f}  {doc.page_content[:80]}")

Metadata filters apply to both the FTS and vector sides:

results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(
    "database query",
    k=10,
    filter={"category": "tech", "year": {"$gte": 2023}},
)

The sync store works the same way:

from langchain_cockroachdb import CockroachDBVectorStore

store = CockroachDBVectorStore(
    engine=engine,
    embeddings=embeddings,
    collection_name="documents",
    hybrid_search_config=HybridSearchConfig(),
)
results = store.similarity_search("distributed databases", k=10)

docs.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (default)
docs.text:
RRF combines results by rank position, ignoring raw scores entirely:

score(doc) = sum(weight / (k + rank(doc))) over both searches

config = HybridSearchConfig(
    fusion_type="reciprocal_rank_fusion",
    k=60,  # RRF constant, higher spreads the top ranks less
)

RRF is the default because ts_rank scores and vector distances live on completely different scales, and rank based fusion sidesteps that problem. It is also what most search engines default to for hybrid retrieval.

Use when:

  • You want a solid default without tuning
  • No strong preference between keyword and semantic matching

docs.title: Weighted Sum
docs.text:
Both score sets are min-max normalized to [0, 1] first, then combined:

final_score = vector_weight * vector_score + fts_weight * fts_score

config = HybridSearchConfig(
    fusion_type="weighted_sum",
    vector_weight=0.7,  # emphasize semantic similarity
    fts_weight=0.3,     # some weight for keywords
)

Use when:

  • You clearly trust one method more than the other
  • You want scores that reflect relative strength, not just rank

docs.title: Weights
docs.text:
Weights apply to both fusion strategies.

# Conceptual queries, synonym matching
HybridSearchConfig(vector_weight=0.8, fts_weight=0.2)

# Exact terms, error codes, technical identifiers
HybridSearchConfig(vector_weight=0.3, fts_weight=0.7)

# General purpose
HybridSearchConfig(vector_weight=0.5, fts_weight=0.5)

docs.title: Candidate pool size
docs.text:
Each search fetches a candidate pool before fusion, max(k * 4, 20) by default. Fetch more when you want fusion to consider a wider net:

results = await vectorstore.asimilarity_search(
    "query",
    k=10,       # return top 10 after fusion
    fetch_k=50, # but pull top 50 from each search first
)

docs.title: Rank normalization for long documents
docs.text:
Raw ts_rank favors long documents. The fts_rank_normalization bitmask is passed straight through to ts_rank to damp that:

# 1 divides by 1 + log(document length), 32 maps ranks to rank / (rank + 1)
config = HybridSearchConfig(fts_rank_normalization=1 | 32)

See the PostgreSQL ts_rank documentation for all flag values.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
The tsvector column and the query must use the same text search configuration. Set it in both places:

await engine.ainit_vectorstore_table(
    table_name="documents",
    vector_dimension=1536,
    create_tsvector=True,
    fts_language="spanish",
)

config = HybridSearchConfig(fts_query_language="spanish")

docs.title: CockroachDB specifics
docs.text:
• Queries are parsed with plainto_tsquery, which ANDs the query terms. CockroachDB does not support websearch_to_tsquery.
  • A query whose keywords match nothing simply contributes an empty FTS list, and you get vector results as usual.
  • The query text is passed to the database as a bound parameter.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Index both sides for large tables:

from langchain_cockroachdb import CSPANNIndex

# Vector index (C-SPANN)
await vectorstore.aapply_vector_index(CSPANNIndex())

# The GIN index for FTS was already created by create_tsvector=True

docs.title: Column does not exist errors on search
docs.text: The table was created without create_tsvector=True. Recreate it, or add the column manually following the SQL shown in Setup.

docs.title: Poor hybrid results
docs.text:
Try the other fusion strategy first, then adjust weights:

config = HybridSearchConfig(fusion_type="weighted_sum", vector_weight=0.8, fts_weight=0.2)

If long documents dominate, set fts_rank_normalization=1 or 1 | 32.

docs.title: No FTS influence on results
docs.text:
plainto_tsquery ANDs all terms, so multi-word queries only produce FTS hits for documents containing every term. Check what the query parses to:

SELECT plainto_tsquery('english', 'your query here');
